Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 1 of 4):

The interpretation of ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿In the name of﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His remembrance be exalted and His names be sanctified, taught His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) good manners by instructing him to mention His beautiful names before all his actions, and He directed him to describe Him by them before all his undertakings [[Taqaddama ilayhi bi-shay': he commanded him to do or undertake it.]]. What He taught him of this, He made from Himself a practice for all His creatures to follow (yastannuna biha) and a path for them to walk upon. Thus, their opening words (awa'il mantiqihim), the beginnings of their letters and books, and their needs are begun with it [[He says: God made that a practice from Him for all His creatures to follow. He placed "from Him" before "for all His creatures."]] [[In the printed edition: "fi iftitah..." and the pronoun in "fabihi" refers to "what He taught him of it."]]. The indication of what is manifest in the speaker's words "In the name of God" suffices to indicate what is hidden of his intended meaning, which is omitted.

This is because the preposition "bi" in "bismi Allah" requires a verb to which it attaches, and no verb appears with it. The hearer of the speaker's "In the name of God" knows his intention, so the speaker does not need to state verbally what he intends, since every speaker who utters it at the start of his speech is, either with it or immediately before it, performing an act that has already informed the hearer of what he began his speech for [[In the printed edition: "min izhar" and "min dalalah shahidah".]]. Thus the hearer's independence from the speaker's explicit statement of the omitted element is like his independence, when he hears someone asked, "What did you eat today?" and he replies, "Food," from the questioner needing to repeat "I ate" with his "food," because the meaning is already clear from the question about what was eaten [[Ma'nahu: i.e., what it means and intends.]]. Therefore it is understood that when a speaker says, "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," and then begins reciting a surah, his following "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" with the recitation of the surah indicates the meaning of his words "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," and it is understood from it that he intends: "I recite in the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." Likewise, when he says "In the name of God" as he rises or sits down and in all his other actions, it indicates the meaning of what he intends by "In the name of God," and that he intended by his words "In the name of God": "I stand in the name of God, I sit in the name of God." The same applies to all other actions.

This which we have said regarding the interpretation of this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Abbas, which:

138 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to us, saying: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from Abdullah ibn Abbas, who said: The first thing Jibril brought down to Muhammad was, he said: "O Muhammad, say: I seek refuge with the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan," then he said: "Say: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." He said: Jibril said to him: Say "In the name of God," O Muhammad, meaning: recite in the remembrance of your Lord, and stand and sit in the remembrance of God. [[Hadith 138 - passed in abridged form with this chain as 137. We have explained it there in detail.]]

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: If the interpretation of His saying "In the name of God" is what you described, and the element that governs the "bi" in "bismi Allah" is what you mentioned, then why is it said "In the name of God," meaning "I recite in the name of God," or "I stand or sit in the name of God"? You know that every reader of the Book of God recites it by God's help and guidance, and every standing, sitting, or acting person stands, sits, and acts by God. Why, given that this is so, is it not said "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," and not just "In the name of God"? For the speaker's saying, "I stand and sit by God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, or I recite by God," is clearer in meaning to the hearer than his saying "In the name of God," since his saying "I stand, I sit in the name of God" may give the hearer the impression that his standing and sitting are in the sense of other than God.

It is said to him, and with God is success: The intended meaning of it is other than what you imagined in yourself. The meaning of His saying "In the name of God" is: I begin by naming God and mentioning Him before everything, or I recite by my naming God, or I stand and sit by my naming God and mentioning Him, not that he means by his saying "In the name of God": I stand by God, or I recite by God, so that the speaker's saying, "I recite by God," or "I stand or sit by God," would be more correct in the way of truth than his saying "In the name of God."

If he says: If the matter is as you described, then why is it said "In the name of God," when you know that "ism" (name) is a name, and "tasmiya" (naming) is a verbal noun from your saying "sammaytu" (I named)?

It is said: The Arabs often bring out verbal nouns in forms that differ from the names, as in their saying: "akramtu Fulanan karamatan" (I honored so-and-so with honor), whereas the pattern of the verbal noun of "af'altu," when derived according to its verb, is "al-if'al." Likewise: "ahantu Fulanan hawanan" (I humiliated so-and-so with humiliation), and "kallamtuhu kalaman" (I spoke to him with speech). The pattern of the verbal noun of "fa''altu" is "al-tafil." Among this is the saying of the poet:

Akufran ba'da radd al-mawti 'anni ... wa ba'da 'ata'ika al-mi'ata al-ri'ata
[[The poem is by al-Qutami, his Diwan: 41, and it comes in the commentary on a verse of Surah Yusuf: 12 (vol. 12 p. 94, Bulaq). He says to Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi, whom he had captured in a war; he showed him favor, gave him a hundred camels, and returned his property. He says: Shall I disbelieve after you have done what you did? "Ata'" here means "i'ta'" (giving), and that is why "al-mi'ah" is in the accusative governed by it. "Al-ri'at" is the plural of "ra'it," meaning camels grazing in a fertile pasture, going and coming.]]
He means: your giving. And from it is the saying of another:

Wa in kana hadha al-bukhlu minka sajiyatan ... laqad kuntu fi tawli raja'ika ash'aba
[[I have not found this verse. Ash'ab: the greedy one, a byword for ravenous greed.]]
He means: in my prolonging of hope in you. And from it is the saying of another:

Azulaymu in musabakum rajulan ... ahda al-salama tahiyyatan zulmu
[[The poem is by al-Harith ibn Khalid al-Makhzumi, al-Aghani 9: 225-226. This is the verse on account of which al-Wathiq summoned Abu Uthman al-Mazini the grammarian to him, and there is a story. See al-Aghani 9: 234 and elsewhere. In the printed edition: "Azlum," the correct reading is from the manuscript, al-Aghani, and al-Shajari's Amali 1: 107 and others. These preceding examples are al-Tabari's evidence that nouns can stand in place of verbal nouns and thus work in the same way in the accusative. Zulaym is the mother of Imran, wife of Abdullah ibn Mut'i, and al-Harith used to court her; when her husband died, he married her.]]
He means: your afflicting. The examples of this meaning are numerous, and what we have mentioned is sufficient for one who is granted understanding of it.

Since it is as we have described, that the Arabs frequently bring out verbal nouns of verbs in forms other than their verbal patterns, and their putting them in the forms of nouns is common and widespread [[He means by his saying "tasdiruha": that they make them verbal nouns from which the verbal acts proceed. This is like your saying "dhahaba dhahaban" (he went with going), where "dhahaba" came from your saying "dhahab" (going), and it then works as a verb. He means that they bring out the verbal noun in the pattern of the noun, so it works as the verb does. Like your saying "al-kalam" is the noun of what you speak with, but they said "kallamtuhu kalaman," placing it in the position of "takllim" (speaking to), and they brought out from "kallama" a verbal noun in the pattern of the noun of what one speaks with, namely "kalam," so the verbal noun is "kalaman."]], it is clear by this the correctness of what we have said in interpreting the saying "In the name of God," that its meaning, when one begins with an action or a speech, is: I begin by naming God before my action or before my speech.

Likewise, the meaning of the speaker's saying at the start of reciting the Qur'an, "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," is only: I recite beginning with the naming of God, or I begin my recitation with the naming of God. Thus "al-ism" (the name) is placed in the position of "al-tasmiya" (naming), just as "al-kalam" is placed in the position of "al-takllim" (speaking to), and "al-'ata'" in the position of "al-i'ta'" (giving).

With the same interpretation as we have said, the report from Abdullah ibn Abbas is narrated:

139 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to us, saying: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from Abdullah ibn Abbas, who said: The first thing Jibril brought down to Muhammad (ﷺ) was, he said: "O Muhammad, say: I seek refuge with the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan," then he said: "Say: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful."

Ibn Abbas said: "In the name of God," Jibril says to him: O Muhammad, recite in the remembrance of your Lord, and stand and sit in the remembrance of God. [[Hadith 139 - this report and its takhrij have passed under number 137.]]

This interpretation by Ibn Abbas indicates the soundness of what we have said: that by the speaker's words beginning his recitation, "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," is meant: I recite by the naming and remembrance of God, and I begin the recitation with the naming of God, with His beautiful names and high attributes. It also clarifies the error of the one who claims that the meaning, from the speaker, is "By God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, the first of everything" [[The words "yuwdhihu" are omitted in the printed edition, which has "awwal kull" and "fi kull" in place of it.]], since the servants are only commanded to begin the openings of their affairs with the naming of God, not with reports of His greatness and attributes, like what they were commanded regarding naming over slaughtered animals and game, at meals and drinks, and in all their other actions. Likewise, what they were commanded regarding naming at the beginning of reciting God's revelation, and at the beginning of their letters and books.

There is no disagreement among all the scholars of the Muslim community that if someone, when slaughtering some livestock, said "By God" and did not say "In the name of God," he would be opposing the sunna by omitting the words "In the name of God" that are prescribed for slaughter. [[Tadhkiya: slaughtering and cutting the throat. Dhakkaytu al-shah tadhkiyatan: I slaughtered the sheep.]] By this it is known that he did not intend by "In the name of God" the words "By God," as the one who claims that the name of God in God's saying "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" is God alleges. For if that were as he claims, then the one who, when slaughtering, says "By God," would have said what is prescribed for him regarding the sacrifice. The consensus of all that the one who says this has abandoned what is prescribed for him over his sacrifice, since he did not say "In the name of God," is a clear proof of the falsity of the interpretation he claimed for the speaker's "In the name of God," that it is meant as "By God," and that the name of God is God.

This is not the place for extended discussion on whether the name is the named or other than it, or is an attribute of it, so that we would lengthen the book with it. This is only a place to clarify the name attached to God: is it a noun, or a verbal noun meaning naming? [[Abu Ja'far, may God be pleased with him, chose the best opinion for his argument. What he wrote before, and what follows after, is among the most accurate of what has been said in explaining this point, over which minds and pens have quarreled. The explanation of what Abu Ja'far said: your saying "ism" in "bismi Allah" is truly a verbal noun (or noun of action). That is, it is in origin a noun for what you do in naming a thing, like "al-kalam," a noun of action for what you do in speaking, and like "al-'ata'," a noun of action for what you do in giving, and like "al-ghusl," a noun of action for what you do in bathing. Its origin seems to be from your saying "sammawtu al-shay' sumuwwan" (I named the thing), and they let its triliteral verb die out and kept its verbal noun "sumuw," then they dropped its final waw so it became "sum," and replaced it with an alif at its beginning, so it became "ism," just as your saying "kalam" comes from a triliteral verb "kalama kalaman," on the pattern of "dhahaba dhahaban." They let the triliteral verb die out, kept its verbal noun "kalam," and made it a noun of action for what you do in speaking. Then they brought out the verbal noun of the quadriliteral in the form of the noun of this action, saying "kallama yukallimu kalaman," meaning "kallama yukallimu takliman."

Likewise they did with their saying "sammá yusammi tasmiyatan": they brought out for this quadriliteral a verbal noun in the form of the noun of action, which is "ism," saying "sammá yusammi ismán," meaning "sammá yusammi tasmiyatan." So your saying "kalam" meaning "takllim" and your saying "ism" meaning "tasmiya" were both brought out in the forms of nouns of action. Therefore, the one added to His name, may He be exalted, in your saying "bismi Allah" and similar expressions, is a verbal noun that came out in the form of a noun of action, from a quadriliteral verb "sammá yusammi," so it has the meaning of its verbal noun, "tasmiya." In this place and similar ones, it means the verbal noun "tasmiya," not the noun of action for what you do in naming. (See: 123-124, al-Tabari's discussion in "Allah.")]]

What Abu Ja'far, may God be pleased with him, said is the most brilliant thing said in explaining this particle from Arabic speech. He reflected well and most precisely, yet it was hidden from the great scholars who spoke about explaining the meaning of "ism" in "bismi Allah" and similar expressions, so they neglected it entirely because of its obscurity and the difficulty of its approach, and because they were accustomed to discussing what they had begun regarding the "name," whether it is the named or something else, or an attribute of it, and what its definition and description are. That is a different topic from what we are concerned with, so they confused it greatly. Then al-Tabari came and sifted out the truth with complete scrutiny, and it is, in our judgment, the most preferable of opinions and the most worthy of precedence, for one who is granted understanding of it, as Abu Ja'far, may God forgive him, says. He will mention after this proof that adds further clarity and explanation to the meaning. Had it not been for fear of lengthening, I would have brought the evidence for preferring al-Tabari's opinion, which they neglected, over every view that preceded it or came after it.

If someone says: What then do you say about the verse of Labid ibn Rabi'a:

"Ila al-hawli, thumma ism al-salami 'alaykuma, ... wa man yabki hawlan kamilan faqad i'tadhar"
[[From his Diwan, poem no. 21, al-Khizana 2: 217, and it will come again in the commentary on a verse of Surah al-Tawba: 90 (10: 144 Bulaq), and a verse of Surah al-Ra'd: 35 (13: 109). The poet says it to his two daughters, when he said: "My two daughters wish that their father would live, and am I not but of Rabi'a or Mudar?" Then he commanded them with his command, saying before the verse of evidence: "So stand and speak of what you know, and do not scratch a face or shave hair," and say: "He is the man who did not abandon his friend, nor betray a companion, nor deceive." So his saying "ila al-hawl..." means: do that until the year turns. "Al-hawl" is the full year entire. His saying "i'tadhar" here means "a'dhar": he reached the utmost extent of excuse.]]
Has the authority in the knowledge of Arabic language interpreted it as meaning: "then the peace be upon you both," and that the name of peace is peace? [[This authority in the knowledge of Arabic language is Abu Ubayda Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna, in his book Majaz al-Qur'an: 16. He fell into a dispute with ... And all that follows is a bitter rebuke from Abu Ja'far to Abu Ubayda.]]

It is said to him: If that were permissible and its interpretation as he interpreted were sound, then it would be permissible to say: "I saw the name of Zayd," "I ate the name of the food," and "I drank the name of the drink." The consensus of all the Arabs on the impossibility of that indicates the falsity of the interpretation of one who interprets Labid's saying "then the name of peace be upon you both" as meaning "then peace be upon you both," claiming that inserting the name and attaching it to peace was permissible only because the name of the named is the named itself.

Those who hold the view of the one whose statement we have quoted are asked: Do you permit in Arabic to say "I ate the name of honey," meaning "I ate honey," just as you permit "the name of peace be upon you," while you mean "peace be upon you"?

If they say: Yes, they have left the language of the Arabs and permitted in its speech what all the Arabs reject in their language. If they say: No, they are asked to state the difference between the two, and they will not say anything about one of them without being bound to the same about the other.

If someone says to us: Then what is your view of this saying of Labid?

It is said to him: It may have two meanings, both different from what the one whose statement we quoted said.

One of them: "al-salam" is one of the names of God, so it is possible that Labid meant by his saying "then the name of peace be upon you both": then keep to the name of God and His remembrance after that, and leave my remembrance and weeping over me, in the sense of urging. He put the noun in the nominative because he delayed the particle that comes to mean urging. [[In the printed edition: "idha wa akhkhara." His saying "fa-raf'a al-ism" means what is in Labid's words "thumma ism," which should have been in the accusative for urging if he had said "thumma 'alaykuma ism al-salam" with the urging placed first.]] The Arabs do this when they delay the urging and put forward the object urged, although they may put it in the accusative even when it is delayed. An example of this is the saying of the poet:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 2 of 4):

Ya ayyuha al-ma'ih dalwi dunaka! ... Inni ra'aytu al-nas yahmadunaka! [This is a rajaz verse from a long report (al-Khizanah 3:17). It was said in mockery of a man whom people threw into a well, and then they recited rajaz about him. Al-ma'ih is the man who descends to the bottom of the well when its water has diminished; he throws the buckets and fills them with his hand, and then bails out for his companions.]

He uses "dunaka" as an imperative with the sense of a verb placed at the end, and what he means is: "dunaka dalwi" (take my bucket). This is the saying of Labid:

ila al-hawli, thumma smu al-salamu 'alaykuma *

meaning: "alaykuma ism al-salam", that is, hold fast to the remembrance of God, and call upon my remembrance and grief over me, for whoever weeps for a full year over a dead man has made his excuse. This is one of its two meanings.

The other meaning of the two: "thumma tasmiyati Allaha 'alaykuma", as one says to a thing he sees and admires, "ism Allah 'alayk", seeking protection thereby from harm, as if he said: "thumma ism Allah 'alaykuma min al-su'" (then the name of God be upon you against evil). It seems that the first meaning is closer to Labid's words. [Without doubt the first is the most correct of the sayings. For he had commanded his two daughters, as we mentioned in his earlier verses, that they should stand to mourn him with what he commanded them of lamentation, eulogy and elegy, and that they should do so from the time he dies until a year passes over him. Therefore there is no sense, after a year, in his conveying greetings to them, that is the greeting of one departing, since he has been separated from them for a full year. It is more fitting for him to pray for them, or to release them from what he commanded them, since they have fulfilled what he commanded in the manner he loved. "And whoever weeps for a full year has made his excuse," as if he said: "Then desist from what I commanded you, for whoever weeps for a year has reached the furthest extent of excuse." So the context of the poem decisively supports the preference of what al-Tabari held in general, and the certainty that the meaning of "thumma ism al-salam 'alaykuma" is: hold fast to the remembrance of God, call upon my remembrance, weep for me, and grieve for me.]

It is said to whoever directs this verse of Labid toward the meaning "thumma al-salam 'alaykuma": do you consider what we have said, of these two meanings, to be permissible, or one of them, or other than what you have said about it?

If he says: "No!", he has shown the extent of his knowledge of the varieties of Arabic speech, and has spared his opponent from debating him.

If he says: "Yes!"

It is said to him: then what is your proof for the correctness of what you claim of the interpretation, that it is the right one, rather than what you mentioned as its possible meaning, from the aspect which we are obliged to accept from you? There is no way to that.

As for the report which:

140 - Ismail ibn al-Fadl narrated it to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn al-Ala' ibn al-Dahhak [who is nicknamed Zabriq] narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Yahya, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from one who narrated to him, from Ibn Mas'ud; and Mis'ar ibn Kidam, from 'Atiyyah, from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Jesus son of Mary, his mother handed him over to the kuttab to teach him. The teacher said to him: write 'bism'. Jesus said to him: What is 'bism'? The teacher said: I do not know! Jesus said: The ba' is the splendour of God, the sin is His radiance, and the mim is His kingdom." [The hadith 140: this is a fabricated hadith with no basis. It is longer than this, and part of it will come under my numbers 145 and 147. al-Tabari separated each section of it in its place, and there is another addition in the explanation of the words "abjad hawwaz", etc. Ibn Hibban al-Hafiz narrated it in full in his Kitab al-Majruhin, in the biography of Isma'il ibn Yahya ibn 'Abd Allah al-Taymi, no. 44, p. 85, and he said of this Isma'il: "He was among those who narrate fabrications from the trustworthy, and what has no basis from the reliable; it is not lawful to narrate from him or to argue with him in any way." Then he gave an example of his lies, narrating the hadith in full from Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Ruzayn al-Attar, from Ibrahim ibn al-Ala' ibn al-Dahhak, with the second chain that is here, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his Tafsir 1:35, quoting Ibn Mardawayh, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id alone, gathering in it the three sections that are separated here. Then he pointed to al-Tabari's narration of it, and then said: "This is very strange, and it may be sound up to someone below the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it may be from the Isra'iliyyat, not from the marfu' reports!" I do not know how the hafiz Ibn Kathir overlooked that this chain contains this liar, so that the report falls outright and does not need this hesitation. As for al-Suyuti, he mentioned it in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:8, attributing it to Ibn Jarir, Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, Ibn 'Asakir in Tarikh Dimashq and al-Tha'labi, and he did not neglect its defect; he mentioned that it is "with a very weak chain". al-Dhahabi wrote the biography of this Isma'il ibn Yahya in al-Mizan 1:117, and Ibn Hajar followed him in Lisan al-Mizan 1:441-442, and in his biography: "Salih ibn Muhammad Jazarah said: he used to fabricate hadith. al-Azdi said: a pillar of lies, it is not lawful to narrate from him... Abu 'Ali al-Nisaburi the hafiz, al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim said: a liar." Ibn Hajar said: "agreed upon its abandonment." He and al-Dhahabi mentioned this hadith as an example of his lies.
Then, his first chain, which Isma'il ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Mulaykah, also contains an unknown narrator, namely "one who narrated to him from Ibn Mas'ud". As for his second chain, which this Isma'il narrated from Mis'ar ibn Kidam, it also contains "'Atiyyah ibn Sa'd ibn Janadah al-'Awfi", who is weak; Ahmad, Abu Hatim and others declared him weak.
The addition between brackets, in the nickname of Ibrahim ibn al-'Ala', is from the manuscript. "Zabriq" is with a kasra on the za' and a silent ya' between the ra' and the qaf; it is the nickname of Ibrahim, it is said. The correct view is that it is the nickname of his father, for al-Bukhari said in his biography in al-Kabir 1/1/307: "Ibrahim claimed that his father was called Zabriq." Ibn Abi Hatim said in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/121: "Ibrahim ibn al-'Ala'... is known as Ibn al-Zabriq."] I fear that it is an error by the narrator, and that he intended [b s m] in the manner in which young children in the kuttab are taught the letters of abjad, and thereby erred, and joined it, saying "bism", since this interpretation has no meaning when one recites "bismillah al-rahman al-rahim" as the reader recites it in the Book of God, because its meaning is impossible according to what all Arabs and the people of their language understand, if its interpretation is taken in that way.

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted be His praise: ﴿Allah﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: As for the interpretation of the words of God, may His remembrance be exalted, "Allah", it is according to the meaning transmitted to us from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: He is the one whom every thing worships (ya'lahuhu) and every creature serves (ya'budu).

141 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umarah narrated to us, saying: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Allah" is the possessor of divinity and worship over all His creatures. [The hadith 141: the chain of this report is weak, as we explained at length in the chain of report 137. What is here was transmitted by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:8, together with its remainder that comes below as no. 148 with the same chain. He attributed it to Ibn Jarir (where he wrote "Ibn Jurayj", a printing error) and Ibn Abi Hatim.]

If someone says to us: Is there for that in the pattern "fa'ala yef'alu" a root from which this name was formed?

It is said: As for hearing from the Arabs, no; but by inference.

If he says: And what indicates that divinity is worship, and that the ilah is the one worshipped, and that it has a root in "fa'ala yef'alu"?

It is said: There is no dispute among the Arabs in judging correct the saying of the speaker, describing a man in worship and in seeking what is with God, may His remembrance be exalted: "ta'allaha fulan" [the man became devoted], without disagreement. Among this is the saying of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

Lillahi darru al-ghaniyati al-mudahhi [Diwan: 165. al-muddah: plural of madah. madda fulanan yamuddahu madhan: he described his appearance and beauty, praised and extolled him. "istarja'na": they said "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un", saying it in grief over him, how he has become ascetic and abandoned the world after what he had of youth, beauty and passion!] sabbahna wa istarja'na min ta'allahi

meaning: from my worship and my seeking of God by my deeds.

There is no doubt that "al-ta'alluh" is the tafa''ul form from "allaha yalhu", and that the meaning of "alaha", when pronounced, is "he worshipped God". A verbal noun has come from it, showing that the Arabs have pronounced it from the pattern "fa'ala yef'alu" without addition.

142 - This is what Sufyan ibn Wakf narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Nafi' ibn 'Umar, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn 'Abbas: that he recited "wa yadharaka wa al-ahatak" [Surah al-A'raf: 127] and said: your worship. It is also said: he was worshipped and did not worship.

143 - Sufyan narrated to us, saying: Ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn al-Hasan, from Ibn 'Abbas: "wa yadharaka wa ilahatak", he said: Pharaoh was only worshipped and did not worship. [The two reports 142 and 143: their chains are weak, because of "Sufyan ibn Wakf ibn al-Jarrah", al-Tabari's teacher in both. This Sufyan was weak; his father was a leading authority, a proof, and he himself was a righteous man, but his copyist corrupted his narrations and inserted into them what was not from his transmission. The scholars advised him to abandon this, but he did not, and for this reason they abandoned him. Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin, no. 470, pp. 238-239: "Because of his persistence in what he was told, he deserved to be abandoned."
These two reports will be mentioned by al-Tabari in his commentary on the verse of Surah al-A'raf: 127 (9:18 Bulaq), and there is some distortion in one of them. al-Suyuti transmitted their meaning in al-Durr al-Manthur 3:107.
The correct, well-known reading is: ﴿wa yadharaka wa alihatak﴾. As for this reading "wa ilahatak", it was transmitted by the author of Ithaf al-Bashar, p. 229, from Ibn Muhaysin and al-Hasan. Ibn Khalawayh transmitted it in al-Qira'at al-Shadhdhah, p. 45, from 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Hayyan mentioned it in al-Bahr 4:367 from these three, "and Anas and a group other than them."]
And so 'Abd Allah and Mujahid used to read it.

144 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Dawud narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj informed me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: concerning His saying "wa yadharaka wa ilahatak", he said: and your worship. [The report 144: al-Husayn ibn Dawud, his name is al-Husayn and his nickname is Sunayd, with a damma on the unpointed sin and a fatha on the nun. He is known by this nickname and is recorded under it in al-Tahdhib 4:244-245, and in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/1/326. Hajjaj is Ibn Muhammad al-Misisi, one of the teachers of Imam Ahmad. This report from Mujahid al-Tabari will narrate in the commentary of the verse of al-A'raf (9:18 Bulaq) by another chain.]
There is no doubt that "al-ilahah", according to the explanation of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "alaha Allah fulan ilahatan" [a man worshipped God with worship], just as one says: "'abada Allah fulan 'ibadatan" and "'abara al-ru'ya 'ibaratan". The statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid shows that "alaha" means "worshipped", and that "al-ilahah" is its verbal noun.
If someone says: If it is permissible to say of one who worships God that he "alahahu" [worshipped Him], according to the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, then how is it obligatory to say, when the reporter wishes to inform about God's entitlement to His servant's worship? It is said: As for narration, there is no narration on this with us; but what is obligatory, by analogy with what came in the report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) which:

145 - Ismail ibn al-Fadl narrated it to us, Ibrahim ibn al-'Ala' narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Yahya, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from one who narrated to him from Ibn Mas'ud; and Mis'ar ibn Kidam, from 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi, from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Jesus, his mother handed him over to the kuttab to teach him, and the teacher said to him: write 'Allah'. Jesus said to him: 'Do you know what Allah is? Allah is the god of gods'." [The hadith 145: it is a hadith with no basis. It is part of the fabricated hadith of which al-Tabari narrated a portion above, 140, with this chain. We explained it fully there.]
- that it be said: Allah, exalted be His majesty, made the servant divine (alaha al-'abd), and the servant made Him divine (alahahu). And that the speech of the speaker "Allah" in Arabic has the origin "al-Ilah".

If someone says: How can that be so, given the difference between their two forms?

It is said: Just as it is permissible that His saying: ﴿But He is Allah, my Lord﴾ [Surah al-Kahf: 38] originally was: "lakin ana, huwa Allahu rabbi" (but I, He is Allah, my Lord), as the poet said:

And you strike me with the glance, you are guilty, / and you blame me, but I do not blame you [lakin iyyaki la aqli]

Al-Adddad of Ibn al-Anbari: 163, and al-Khizanah 4:490, and he said: "I have not found its continuation or its speaker, though it is famous, rarely does any grammar book lack it, and God knows best."

He means: "lakin ana iyyaka la aqli" (but I, you I do not blame). He dropped the hamza of "ana", so the nun of "ana" met the nun of "lakin", which was quiescent, and it was assimilated into the nun of "ana", so they became one doubled nun. Likewise "Allah" originally was "al-Ilah"; the hamza, which is the first radical of the noun, was dropped, so the lam which is the middle radical of the noun met the added lam which had entered with the added alif, and it was quiescent, so it was assimilated into the other, which is the middle radical of the noun, and they became in pronunciation one doubled lam, as we described in God's saying ﴿But He is Allah, my Lord﴾.

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted be His praise: ﴿al-Rahman al-Rahim﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: As for "al-Rahman", it is fa'lan, from rahima, and "al-Rahim" is fa'il from it. The Arabs very often form nouns from "fa'ila yef'alu" into "fa'lan", as they say from ghadiba: ghadban, from sakira: sakran, from 'atisha: 'atshan. Likewise their saying "Rahman" from rahima, since the "fa'ila" form of it is: rahima yarhamu. And "Rahim" was said, though the middle vowel of "fa'ila" in it is kasra, because it is praise. It is the habit of the Arabs to put the forms of nouns, when there is praise or blame in them, into the pattern "fa'il", even if the middle vowel of "fa'ila" or "fa'ala" in them is kasra or fatha, as they said from "'alima": 'alim and 'alim, and from "qadara": qadir and qadir. That is not a formation on their verbs, because the formation from "fa'ila yef'alu" and "fa'ala yef'ilu" is fa'il. Had "al-Rahman and al-Rahim" been outside the formation of their verbs, their form would have been "al-Rahim" (the merciful, with the alif).

If someone says: If al-Rahman and al-Rahim are two names derived from mercy, what is the purpose of repeating this, when one of them conveys the meaning of the other?

It is said to him: The matter is not as you suppose; rather, each of the two words has a meaning which the other does not convey.

If he says: And what is the meaning in which each of them is distinct, such that one does not convey the meaning of the other?

It is said: As for the linguistic aspect, there is no dispute [la tamanu': no disagreement among them, prompting some to reject what the other says] among those who know the languages of the Arabs, that the saying of the speaker "al-Rahman", from the forms of nouns of "fa'ila yef'alu", is more deviant than his saying "al-Rahim". And there is no disagreement among them that every noun that had a root in "fa'ila yef'alu", and then deviated from its root of "fa'ila yef'alu" to a greater degree, the one described by it is more excellent than the one described by the noun formed on its root of "fa'ila yef'alu", when the naming by it is praise or blame. This is what the saying "al-Rahman" has, of added meaning over "al-Rahim" in the language.

As for the aspect of report and tradition, there is among the people of interpretation a difference of opinion in it:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 3 of 4):

146. Al-Sarri ibn Yahya al-Tamimi related to me, saying: Uthman ibn Zafar related to us, saying: I heard al-ʿArzami (ʿArzamī) say, regarding "al-Rahman al-Rahim": "Al-Rahman" is for all creation, and "al-Rahim" is for the believers. [[Narration 146: Ibn Kathir cited this place in his Tafsir (1:40). Al-Sarri ibn Yahya ibn al-Sarri al-Tamimi al-Kufi, a shaykh of al-Tabari, appears only in Ibn Abi Hatim's Jarh wa al-Ta'dil (2/1/285), which says: "We were not granted to hear from him directly, and he wrote to us some of his narrations; he was truthful (sadduq)." The al-ʿArzami from whom this statement is related here is very weak. Ahmad (ibn Hanbal) said in his Musnad (6938): "His narrations are not worth anything." He is Muhammad ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Sulayman al-ʿArzami. As for his paternal uncle, Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman al-ʿArzami, he was a reliable Successor (tabiʿi), but early; he died in 145 AH, and Uthman ibn Zafar, who died in 218 AH, did not meet him. The nisba "al-ʿArzami" is with an unpointed ʿayn, a sukun on the rāʾ, and a zāy after it, attributed to ʿArzam. The text here in al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir has "al-ʿArzami" with the zāy placed before the rāʾ, which is a scribal error.]]

147. Ismail ibn al-Fadl related to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn al-ʿAla' related to us, saying: Ismail ibn Ayyash related to us, from Ismail ibn Yahya, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from someone who narrated to him, from Ibn Masʿud; and Misʿar ibn Kidam, from Atiyya al-ʿAwfi, from Abu Saʿid, meaning al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Isa ibn Maryam said: 'Al-Rahman is the Rahman of the Hereafter and this world, and al-Rahim is the Rahim of the Hereafter.'" [[Narration 147: This is a weak isnad, rather two weak isnads, as we explained earlier at 140 and 145.]]

These two reports indicate the difference between naming God by His name "Rahman" and naming Him by His name "Rahim," and the difference in meaning between the two words, even though they differ about the nature of that difference: one indicates that it refers to this world, and the other indicates that it refers to the Hereafter.

If someone asks: "Which of these two interpretations (taʾwil) do you consider more correct?" It is said: Both have a valid basis in soundness for us, so there is no point in asking which of them is more correct. The meaning in naming God as Rahman, as distinct from naming Him as Rahim, is that by the name Rahman He is described as having the all-encompassing mercy toward all His creatures, and by the name Rahim He is described as having a specific mercy toward some of His creatures, either in all circumstances or in some circumstances. Thus, if that is the case, there is no doubt that the specificity in His description as Rahim does not contradict its meaning, whether that is in this world, in the Hereafter, or in both.

If what we have said is correct, and God, may His praise be exalted, has specified His servants the believers in this immediate world with what He has kindly granted them of His success in obeying Him, believing in Him and His messengers, following His command and avoiding His disobedience, which He withheld from those who associated partners with Him, disbelieved, opposed what He commanded them, and committed His prohibitions; and if, along with that, He, may His praise be exalted, has made what He prepared in the later Hereafter in His gardens of lasting bliss and clear triumph exclusively for those who believe in Him, affirm His messengers and act in obedience to Him, to the exclusion of those who associate partners with Him and disbelieve in Him, [[This is the answer to the phrase "since it is correct..." and what lies between them is a digression.]] then it is clear that God has specified the believers with His mercy in this world and the Hereafter, along with the bounty and benevolence that He has extended to all of them, including the believers and the disbelievers in this world, in the expansion of provision, the driving of clouds with rain, the bringing forth of plants from the earth, the health of bodies and minds, and all the other countless blessings shared by believers and disbelievers.

So our Lord, may His praise be exalted, is Rahman to all His creation in this world and the Hereafter, and Rahim specifically to the believers in this world and the Hereafter. As for what He has extended to all of them of His mercy in this world, by which He is Rahman to them, it is what we have mentioned together with its counterparts, which no one among His creatures can count, as He, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿And if you were to count the favor of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Surah Ibrahim: 34; Surah al-Nahl: 18].

As for the Hereafter, what He extends to all of them of His mercy there, by which He is Rahman to them, is His equal treatment of all of them, may His remembrance be exalted, in His justice and judgment: He does not wrong anyone of them by an atom's weight, and if it is a good deed He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward, and every soul will be paid in full for what it has earned. That is the meaning of His generality toward all of them in the Hereafter with His mercy, by which He is Rahman in the Hereafter.

As for what He specified for the believers in this immediate world of His mercy, by which He is Rahim to them in it, as He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿And He is ever merciful to the believers﴾ [Surah al-Ahzab: 43], it is what we described of the gentle guidance He gives them in their religion, which He singled them out with, to the exclusion of those whom He forsook among the people of disbelief.

As for what He specified for them in the Hereafter, by which He is Rahim to them to the exclusion of the disbelievers, it is what we described just now of what He has prepared for them, to the exclusion of others, of bliss and honor beyond the reach of wishes.

As for the other statement regarding its interpretation, it is what:

148. Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Uthman ibn Saʿid related to us, saying: Bishr ibn Umara related to us, saying: Abu Rawq related to us, from al-Dahhak, from Abdullah ibn Abbas, who said: "Al-Rahman" is the form of the verb from mercy (rahma), and it is from the speech of the Arabs. He said: "Al-Rahman al-Rahim" means: gentle and kind to whoever wishes to be shown mercy, and firm and severe toward whoever wishes to be treated harshly. [[Narration 148: Ibn Kathir cited this place in his Tafsir (1:41). The discussion of this isnad and its weakness has already passed (137, 141). In al-Durr al-Manthur (1:8–9) the text reads "toward whoever wishes the punishment to be increased on him," and it appears that this is a change made by a copyist or printer.]] And likewise all His names.

This interpretation from Ibn Abbas shows that what makes our Lord Rahman is also what makes Him Rahim, although the word "al-Rahman" has a meaning that "al-Rahim" does not. For he made the meaning of "al-Rahman" equal to gentle toward whoever is gentle toward Him, and the meaning of "al-Rahim" equal to kind toward whoever is kind to Him.

The statement we related about its interpretation from the Prophet (ﷺ), and mentioned from al-ʿArzami [[A reference to what passed at 146. The text here again has "al-ʿArzami" with the zāy placed before the rāʾ, which is an error, as we explained earlier.]], is more similar to its intended meaning than this statement we related from Ibn Abbas, even though this statement agrees in meaning with that one in that "al-Rahman" has a meaning that "al-Rahim" does not, and that "al-Rahim" has an interpretation other than that of "al-Rahman."

The third statement regarding its interpretation is what:

149. Imran ibn Bakkar al-Kalla'i related to me, saying: Yahya ibn Salih related to us, saying: Abu al-Azhar Nasr ibn Amr al-Lakhmi, from the people of Filastin, related to us, saying: I heard Ata al-Khurasani say: "It was 'al-Rahman.' Then when 'al-Rahman' was cut from His name, it became 'al-Rahman al-Rahim.'" [[Narration 149: Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:9) and attributed it to al-Tabari alone. Ata al-Khurasani is Ata ibn Abi Muslim, who is reliable, though some imams criticized him. He narrated much from the Successors and often narrated with mursal reports from the Companions, and there is disagreement about whether he heard from them. As for the narrator from him, Abu al-Azhar Nasr ibn Amr al-Lakhmi, I have not found a biography for him in the sources available to me, except the statement of al-Dawlabi in al-Kuna wa al-Asma' (1:110): "Abu al-Azhar al-Filastini Nasr ibn Amr al-Lakhmi, from whom Yahya ibn Salih al-Wuhazi narrated."]]

What Ata intended by this statement, God willing, is that "al-Rahman" was among the names of God that no one among His creatures may be called by. When Musaylima the liar named himself with it, which is "cutting it off" from His names (that is, taking part of His names for himself), God, may His praise be exalted, informed that His name is "al-Rahman al-Rahim," so that by this He distinguishes His name for His servants from the name of one who has named himself with His names, since no one is named "al-Rahman al-Rahim," and these two names are not combined for anyone other than Him, may His remembrance be exalted. Rather, some of His creatures may be named "Rahim" or may be named "Rahman," but "Rahman Rahim" has never been combined for anyone other than Him, and they are not combined for anyone other than Him. So the meaning of Ata's statement seems to be that God, may His praise be exalted, distinguished His name from the names of others among His creatures by repeating "al-Rahim" after "al-Rahman," whether their meanings differ or agree.

What Ata said is not corrupt in meaning. Rather, it is possible that God, may His praise be exalted, specified Himself with both names together, to set Himself apart from His creation, so that His servants may know by mentioning them together that He is the one intended by them, to the exclusion of anyone else among His creatures, along with the meaning in the interpretation of each of them that is not in the other.

Some people of dullness have claimed that the Arabs did not know "al-Rahman," and that it was not part of their language. [[The people of dullness in our time still write this and boast of it in their lectures and books, quoting what has been dropped from the sayings, and they are the non-Arabs who compose in what they do not know well, under the name of Orientalism. Al-Tabari's refutation is decisive for anyone who has, out of ignorance and error, a refusal that restrains him from obstinacy.]] That is why the polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And what is al-Rahman? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ [Surah al-Furqan: 60], denying this name, as though it were impossible for them to deny what they knew to be true. Or: ... and as though he had not recited from the Book of God the saying of God: ﴿Those whom We gave the Scripture recognize him as they recognize their sons﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 146], meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), while they nonetheless deny him and reject his prophethood! Thus he would know that they were resisting the reality of what had been firmly established in their own knowledge. And there is a verse recited by one of the foolish pre-Islamic poets:

Did that girl not strike her hybrid camel?
Did al-Rahman, my Lord, not cut off its right hand? [[I have not found the author of this verse. Ibn Sidah cited it in al-Mukhassas (17:152), and Muhammad Mahmud al-Turkuzi al-Shinqiti commented on it, claiming that the verse is fabricated, that "some men who love to find nonexistent evidence for their bare claims made it up and fabricated it," and that the fabrication and artificiality in it are as clear as the sun at midday, and its weakness loudly declares its fabrication. He held that the correct and consensually agreed view is that the pre-Islamic poet referred to is al-Shanfara al-Azdi, and this verse is not in his poetry, and that it is cobbled together from al-Shanfara's saying: "Would that I knew, though regret is misguidance, what the hand of the girl struck of her hybrid camel." Al-Shinqiti, may God have mercy on him, was quick to show off his knowledge and his narrations. What he said about the claim of fabrication cannot stand. The verse that follows it is enough evidence against his claim that the motive for its fabrication was to invent nonexistent evidence for bare claims. There is no weakness or artificiality in the verse.]]

And Salama ibn Jandal al-Saʿdi said: [[In the manuscript and the printed edition, "al-Tuhawi" appears in place of "al-Saʿdi," which is an error. Salama was not from Tuhaw.]]
You hurried against us, so we hurried against you,
And whatever al-Rahman wills, He binds or releases. [[His Diwan (p. 19). He appears in Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shuʿara' (p. 131) with the lineage "Salama ibn Jandal ibn Abd al-Rahman." This is the narration of Ibn Sallam, while others say "ibn Abd." If Ibn Sallam's narration is correct, it is another strong proof against al-Shinqiti's claim.]]

Also, some who had weak knowledge of the interpretation of the interpreters, and little narration of the sayings of the early scholars of exegesis, claimed that "al-Rahman" means "possessor of mercy" (dhu al-rahma), and "al-Rahim" means "one who shows mercy" (al-rahim). [[The one al-Tabari means is Abu Ubayda Mamar ibn al-Muthanna in his book Majaz al-Qur'an (p. 21), and he quoted most of what follows verbatim.]] Then he said: They sometimes derive two words from one root with the same meaning, because speech is broad to them. He said: They did the same, saying "nadman" and "nadim" [companion]. Then he cited the verse of Burj ibn Musahhir al-Ta'i:

And a companion who increases the cup's pleasure, I poured for him when the stars had sunk. [[Hamasa of Abu Tammam (3:135) and al-Mu'talif wa al-Mukhtalif of al-Amidi (p. 62).]]

He cited similar verses with "nadim" and "nadman," thus distinguishing the meanings of "al-Rahman" and "al-Rahim" in interpretation, saying "al-Rahman" is "possessor of mercy" and "al-Rahim" is "one who shows mercy." Yet he left the explanation of their two meanings in a sound form. Then he illustrated this with two words that come from one root with one meaning, returning to what he had made into two meanings, and making it an example of one meaning with different words.

There is no doubt that "possessor of mercy" is one for whom mercy is established and whose attribute of mercy is confirmed, and that "one who shows mercy" is one described as going to show mercy, or who has shown mercy so that it is past, or who is in the state of it. But there is no indication in it that mercy is an attribute of Him, as there would be if He were described as "possessor of mercy." So where is the meaning of "al-Rahman al-Rahim" in his interpretation, compared with the meaning of two words that come as derivatives from one root with different forms but agreeing in meaning? But when a statement has no reliable foundation, its flaw becomes clear.

If someone asks us: "Why did He put the name of God, which is 'Allah,' before His name 'al-Rahman,' and His name 'al-Rahman' before His name 'al-Rahim'?"

It is said: Because it is the way of the Arabs, when they wish to inform about the one being informed about, to put his name first, then follow it with his attributes and descriptions. This is the required form in judgment: the name should come before its description and attribute, so that the listener knows the information and whom it concerns. When that is the case, and God, may His remembrance be exalted, has names that He has forbidden His creatures to be named with, which He has specified for Himself to the exclusion of them, such as "Allah," "al-Rahman," and "al-Khaliq"; and names that He has permitted them to name one another with, such as al-Rahim, al-Sami', al-Basir, al-Karim, and similar names, then it is necessary that His names which are exclusively His, to the exclusion of all His creatures, be put first, so that the listener knows to whom praise and glorification are directed. Then his names by which others have been named are followed, after the listener or addressee knows whom the meanings that follow refer to. God, may His remembrance be exalted, began with His name "Allah," because divinity belongs to no one other than Him, may His praise be exalted, in any respect, neither in the sense of being named by it nor in the sense of its meaning. We have explained that the meaning of "Allah," may He be exalted in remembrance, is the One worshipped [[In the printed edition: "the meaning of Allah is the One worshipped."]], and there is no one worthy of worship except Him, may His majesty be exalted, and that naming oneself with it has been forbidden by God, may His praise be exalted, even if the one who names himself with it intends what one intends by naming someone "Sa'id" [the happy] while he is miserable, or "Hasan" [the good] while he is ugly.

Do you not see that God, may His majesty be exalted, said in more than one verse of His Book: ﴿Is there a god with God?﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 60], and it is considered a great thing for one who affirms it? And He, may He be exalted, specified Himself by "Allah" and "al-Rahman" when He said: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon al-Rahman; whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [Surah al-Isra': 110]. Then He paired His name "al-Rahman" with it, since He had also forbidden His creatures to name themselves with it, although among His creatures there are those who may deserve to be named by some of its meanings. For it is permissible to describe many of those who are below God among His creatures with some attributes of mercy. But it is not permissible for anyone other than Him to deserve any part of divinity. That is why "al-Rahman" came second after His name "Allah."

As for His name "al-Rahim," we have mentioned that it is permissible to describe others with it. Mercy is one of His attributes, may His remembrance be exalted, so when the matter is as we have described, it stands in the position of the attributes of names, which follow them after the names precede them. This is the reason for placing the name of God "Allah" before His name "al-Rahman," and His name "al-Rahman" before His name "al-Rahim." [[This argument is among the best that has been said, and its precision shows the good judgment of Abu Ja'far regarding what presents itself to him. His whole tafsir is evidence of this. May God have mercy on him.]]

And al-Hasan al-Basri used to say about "al-Rahman" the same as what we have said: that it is one of the names of God that He forbade His servants to name themselves with. [[In the printed edition they changed it to "for His servants."]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 4 of 4):

150. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Mas'adah narrated to us, from Awf, from al-Hasan, who said: "Al-Rahman" is a forbidden name. [[Narration 150: Ibn Kathir quoted it in his Tafsir (1:41-42) from this passage. Al-Suyuti, in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:9), attributed it to al-Tabari alone. "Awf," the narrator from al-Hasan, is Awf ibn Abi Jamilah al-Abdi, known as Ibn al-A'rabi, and he is trustworthy and firm (thiqah thabt).]]

Indeed, the consensus (ijma', the agreement of the Muslim community) that it is forbidden for all people to name themselves by it is sufficient, without needing to cite the saying of al-Hasan and others to support what we have said on this matter.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):**

**The discussion on the interpretation of the Opening (al-Fatiha)**

﴿All praise is due to God﴾:

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of ﴿All praise is due to God﴾ is: gratitude belongs exclusively to God, may His praise be exalted, to the exclusion of all that is worshipped besides Him, and of everything He has created [In the printed edition: "ma yura" (what is seen); the correct reading, from the manuscript and Ibn Kathir 1:42, is "ma bara'a" (what He has created)]. This is for the blessings He has bestowed upon His servants, which no number can count and no one other than Him can encompass: in the soundness of their faculties for obedience, in enabling the limbs of the bodies of the responsible (mukallafun) to perform His obligations, together with the provision He has extended to them in their worldly life and the pleasant sustenance with which He has nourished them, without them having any claim upon Him for it, and together with what He has pointed them to and called them towards, of the means leading to everlasting abiding in the abode of lasting bliss. So to our Lord belongs praise for all of this, first and last.

In accordance with what we have mentioned of the interpretation of the saying of our Lord, may His remembrance be exalted and His names be sanctified, ﴿All praise is due to God﴾, there has come a report from Ibn 'Abbas and others:

151. Muhammad ibn al-'Ala' told us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id told us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara told us, saying: Abu Rawq told us, on the authority of al-Dahhak, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Gabriel said to Muhammad (peace and blessings of God be upon them both): "Say, O Muhammad, 'All praise is due to God.'" Ibn 'Abbas said: "'All praise is due to God' is: gratitude to God, submission to God, acknowledgement of His blessing, His guidance, His beginning of favours, and other than that."

[Hadith 151: The chain of this isnad was previously shown to be weak at (137). "Muhammad ibn al-'Ala'", the teacher of al-Tabari, is "Abu Kurayb" himself in the preceding chain, sometimes named and sometimes given the kunya. This hadith was transmitted by Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir 1:43, by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:11, and by al-Shawkani in his tafsir called Fath al-Qadir 1:10, and they also attributed it to Ibn Abi Hatim in his tafsir.]

152. And Sa'id ibn 'Amr al-Sakuni told me, saying: Baqiyya ibn al-Walid told us, saying: 'Isa ibn Ibrahim told me, on the authority of Musa ibn Abi Habib, on the authority of al-Hakam ibn 'Umayr, who had companionship (with the Prophet), who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you say 'All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds', you have thanked God, and He will increase you."

[Hadith 152: Ibn Kathir transmitted it at 1:43 with al-Tabari's isnad, and al-Suyuti mentioned it in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:11, attributing it to al-Tabari, al-Hakim in Tarikh Nisabur, and al-Daylami, "with a weak chain". The isnad is truly weak, indeed it is an isnad with no leg to stand on, as we will mention:
As for Baqiyya ibn al-Walid, the truth is that he is trustworthy (thiqa); they criticised him only for tadlis (concealment of sources), which has no place here, since he explicitly stated the transmission ("haddathani").
But 'Isa ibn Ibrahim, the Qurashi Hashimi, is the entire source of the calamity in this hadith and in hadiths of a similar kind that he transmitted by this isnad. Al-Bukhari said of him in al-Du'afa' (p. 27): "munkar al-hadith" (rejected in hadith), and so did al-Nasa'i (p. 22). Ibn Abi Hatim included him in al-Jarh wa-l-Ta'dil 3/1: 271–272, and transmitted from his father that he said: "matruk al-hadith" (abandoned in hadith), and from Ibn Ma'in: "laysa bi-shay'" (he is nothing). Ibn Hibban said in al-Du'afa', folio 163: "It is not permissible to argue with him if he is alone." His biography in al-Mizan and Lisan al-Mizan contains wonders.
His teacher Musa ibn Abi Habib is like him: weak and destroyed. Al-Dhahabi said in al-Mizan: "Abu Hatim criticised him, and his report is discarded. He has (a report) from al-Hakam ibn 'Umayr, a man said to have had companionship. What I see is that he did not meet him. Musa, despite his weakness, is later than meeting a great companion." So the calamity is from these two, or from one of them.
To the point that some memorisers doubted the existence of the companion himself, "al-Hakam ibn 'Umayr", because of these two! Ibn Abi Hatim included him in al-Jarh wa-l-Ta'dil 1/2/125, saying: "al-Hakam ibn 'Umayr: he transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ); he does not mention hearing or meeting, (he narrated) rejected hadiths, from the transmission of his nephew Musa ibn Abi Habib, who is a weak sheikh in hadith, and 'Isa ibn Ibrahim transmits from Musa ibn Abi Habib, and he is one whose hadith is lost; I heard my father say that."
Indeed al-Dhahabi denied his companionship and included him in al-Mizan, and erred in quoting from Abu Hatim, mentioning that he weakened al-Hakam! But Abu Hatim's words, as you see, are otherwise. The Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) responded to him in Lisan al-Mizan 2:337 and established that he was a companion, on the basis of what Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Ibn Mandah, Abu Nu'aym, al-Tirmidhi and others mentioned, and that al-Daraqutni said: "He was a Badri" (a veteran of Badr).
Ibn Hibban mentioned him in Kitab al-Thiqat (p. 54) in the class of the companions, and said: "It is said he had companionship." The Hafiz transmitted this in al-Lisan from Ibn Hibban, but he erred, claiming that he mentioned him among "the trustworthy Successors".
Ibn 'Abd al-Barr included him in al-Isti'ab, no. 476, under the name "al-Hakam ibn 'Amr al-Thumali; Thumala is among the Azd; he witnessed Badr, and strange hadiths are transmitted from him, from the hadiths of the people of Syria, which are not sound." The naming of his father as "'Amr" is an old error in the copies of al-Isti'ab, because Ibn al-Athir followed him in Usd al-Ghaba 1:26 and pointed out the error, then included him correctly: "al-Hakam ibn 'Umayr al-Thumali, from the Azd, and he used to live in Homs." The Hafiz investigated his biography well in al-Isaba 2:30.]

He said: And it has been said: the saying of the one who says "All praise is due to God" is a laudation of God by His names and His most beautiful attributes; and his saying "Gratitude is due to God" is a laudation of Him by His blessings and His favours.

It has been transmitted from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: "'All praise is due to God' is a laudation of God." But the report from him did not make clear which of the two meanings of laudation we have mentioned it refers to.

153. Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la al-Sadafi told us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: 'Umar ibn Muhammad told me, on the authority of Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, on the authority of his father, who said: al-Sulami informed me, on the authority of Ka'b, who said: Whoever says "All praise is due to God", that is a laudation of God.

[Report 153: This isnad is sound, but whether it is sound or weak, it has no value, since its endpoint is Ka'b al-Ahbar. The words of Ka'b were never a proof, in tafsir or otherwise. "al-Sadafi" with the sad and dal unpointed, a nisba to "Sadaf" with a fatha on the sad and a kasra on the dal, a tribe of Himyar that settled in Egypt. "al-Sulami" is 'Abd Allah ibn Damra al-Sulami, a trustworthy Successor.
Ibn Kathir mentioned this report from Ka'b at 1:43 without an isnad or attribution. Al-Suyuti mentioned it at 1:11, attributing it to al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim.]

154. 'Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Kharraz told me, saying: Muslim ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jarmi told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Mus'ab al-Qurqsani told us, on the authority of Mubarak ibn Fadala, on the authority of al-Hasan, on the authority of al-Aswad ibn Sari': that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Nothing is more beloved to Him, from God, than praise, and for that reason He praised Himself, saying: 'All praise is due to God.'"

[Hadith 154: Its isnad is sound. 'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Abdawayh Abu al-Hasan al-Kharraz, the teacher of al-Tabari, is trustworthy, biographed in Tarikh Baghdad 11:374–375. "al-Kharraz" is firmly recorded in al-Tabari with a kha and a ra and a final zay. In Tarikh Baghdad it is "al-Khazzaz" with two zays, and we could not decide between them. Muslim ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jarmi: biographed in Lisan al-Mizan 6:32 under the name "Muslim ibn Abi Muslim", without mention of his father's name, and he is the same person. Al-Khatib included him in Tarikh Baghdad 13:100, saying: "Muslim ibn Abi Muslim al-Jarmi, and he is Muslim ibn 'Abd al-Rahman", and said: "He was trustworthy; he settled in Tarsus, and his death was there." "al-Jarmi" was written in the originals of al-Tabari and in Lisan al-Mizan as "al-Harmi" without dots. But they did not state its vocalisation. Their custom in such matters is to state the vocalisation of the rare and anomalous, and to leave the common form which is standard in vocalisation; the standard form of this writing is "al-Jarmi" with a jim, and it is so written in Tarikh Baghdad, so we preferred this or that. "Muhammad ibn Mus'ab al-Qurqsani" and "Mubarak ibn Fadala" are disputed. We have preferred their authentication in the commentary on the Musnad: the first at 3048, and the second at 521. "al-Hasan" is al-Basri, and we established in the commentary on Sahih Ibn Hibban, at hadith 132, that he heard from al-Aswad ibn Sari'.
Al-Suyuti mentioned this hadith in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:12 from the tafsir of al-Tabari. Ahmad transmitted it in the Musnad in an abridged form in similar meaning, no. 15650 (3:435, Halabi), from Rawh ibn 'Ubada, on the authority of 'Awf ibn Abi Jamila, on the authority of al-Hasan, on the authority of al-Aswad ibn Sari', who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, shall I not recite to you praises with which I have praised my Lord? He said: Indeed your Lord loves praise." This isnad is sound; all its narrators are trustworthy and firm. Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his tafsir 1:43 from the Musnad. Likewise al-Suyuti mentioned it and attributed it also to al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim and others.
Ahmad also transmitted it, no. 15654, and al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, p. 51, in similar form, in a lengthy story, from the narration of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra on the authority of al-Aswad ibn Sari'.
Its meaning is established and sound, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud in the Musnad, no. 4153: "No one is more jealous than God, and for that reason He forbade indecencies, whether apparent or hidden; and no one loves praise more than God, and for that reason He praised Himself." It was also transmitted by al-Bukhari, Muslim and others.]

Abu Ja'far said: There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge of the Arabic language, as a rule, regarding the saying of the speaker "All praise is due to God, gratitude" being correct. So it is clear, since that is correct according to all of them, that "al-hamdu lillah" may be uttered in the place of gratitude, and that gratitude may be placed in the place of praise. For if that were not so, it would not be permissible to say "al-hamdu lillahi shukran", and it would produce from the saying of the speaker "al-hamdu lillah" a verbal noun (masdar) of "ashkuru" (I thank), because if gratitude did not mean praise, it would be an error for a meaning other than its meaning and its wording to be produced from praise.

[Note: The scholars have discussed refuting what Abu Ja'far held, that "praise" (hamd) and "gratitude" (shukr) have the same meaning, and that one may be placed in the place of the other; this is also what al-Mubarrad held. See al-Qurtubi 1:116 and Ibn Kathir 1:42. The citation from al-Qurtubi was mistaken: one took him to be citing in support of al-Tabari's view, which is an error. What al-Tabari said is the stronger proof and the more ancient Arabic than those who contradicted him. His phrase "masdar ashkur" and his phrase "to be produced from praise" mean the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). See what has passed: (117), footnote 1.]

If one of us were to say: What is the reason for the insertion of the alif and lam in al-hamd? Why not say: "hamdan lillahi rabbi al-'alamin" (praise to God, Lord of the worlds)?

It is said: For the insertion of the alif and lam in al-hamd, there is a meaning that the saying "hamdan", with the omission of the alif and lam, does not convey. That is because their insertion in al-hamd indicates that its meaning is [In the printed edition: "mabni 'ala anna ma'nahu" (based on the fact that its meaning is); they have introduced a change into it]: all praises and complete gratitude belong to God. And if they were removed from it, it would indicate only that the praise of the one who says it belongs to God, and not all praises. For the meaning of the saying "hamdan lillah" or "hamdun lillah" is: "I praise God with praise", and the interpretation of the saying of the one who recites the Mother of the Qur'an, ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, is not "I praise God", but rather the interpretation of it is what we described earlier, that all praises belong to God by His divinity and by His bestowing blessings upon His creation with the blessings He has bestowed upon them, which have no equal in religion and in the world, and in the immediate and the deferred.

And on account of this meaning, the recitation of the reciters and the scholars of the community has followed one course, in raising "al-hamd" in ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, rather than putting it in the accusative, which would lead to indicating that the meaning of what follows is likewise: "I praise God with praise". If a reciter were to recite it in the accusative, its meaning would, in my view, be invalidated, and he would deserve punishment for reciting it thus, if he deliberately recited it so, knowing its error and the corruption of its interpretation.

If one of us were to say: And what is the meaning of His saying "al-hamdu lillah"? Did God Himself praise Himself, may His praise be exalted, and laud Himself, and then teach it to us so that we would say it as He said it and described Himself with it? If that is so, what is the purpose, then, of His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, when He, mighty is His remembrance, is the one worshipped, not the worshipper? Or is that the speech of Gabriel or of Muhammad, the Messenger of God (ﷺ)? Then it has been shown false that this is God's speech.

It is said: Rather, all of that is the speech of God, may His praise be exalted, but He, may His remembrance be exalted, praised Himself and lauded Himself with what He is worthy of, then taught that to His servants, and made its recitation obligatory upon them, as a test from Him for them and a trial. So He said to them: Say ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, and say ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾. So His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ is among what He, may His remembrance be exalted, taught them to say and to submit to its meaning. And that is connected with His saying ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, as if He said: Say this, and this.

If one says: And where is His saying "say" (qulu), so that the interpretation of that would be what you claim?

It is said: We have shown previously that the Arabs' custom, when they know the place of a word, and are not in doubt that the listener knows, by what they have shown in their speech, what they have omitted, is to omit what the apparent part of their speech suffices for, especially if that omitted word is a saying, or the interpretation of a saying, as the poet said:

I know that I will be a mound (ramsan) when the swift camels travel, and it does not travel.

[The verse is found in the interpretation of the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun: 87 (18:27 Bulaq), and it is attributed to some of the Banu 'Amir, and likewise in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:170. Both are in al-Bayan wa-l-Tabyin 3:184, attributed to al-Wuzayri, whom I did not identify, and there is variation in the transmission. "Ramas": the grave levelled over with earth. He means: he will become a grave that is visited or lamented over. Al-Jahiz transmitted it as "sa-asir mayyitan" (I will become a dead man), which is nothing. "al-Nawa'ij" is the plural of "na'ija", meaning swift camels, which "na'ajat" in their travel, that is, they travelled in every direction from their vigour. In al-Bayan and al-Farra's Ma'ani it is "al-nawaji'", and that is nothing.]

The askers said: For whom did you dig?
And the informers said to them: "a vizier."

[The narration of al-Jahiz: "The askers said: Who is covered?" In al-Ma'ani it is "al-sa'irun" (the travellers).]

Abu Ja'far said: He means by that: the informers said to them: the dead one is a vizier. So he omitted "the dead one" because he had already brought in speech what indicated it. Likewise the saying of another:

And you saw your husband in battle, girded with a sword and a spear.

[This is found in the interpretation of verses of Surat al-Baqara: 7, and Surat Al 'Imran: 49, and Surat al-Ma'ida: 53, and Surat al-An'am: 99, and Surat al-Anfal: 14, and Surat Yunus: 71, and Surat al-Rahman: 22. It is a verse cited in every book.]

It is known that the spear is not girded, and he only meant: carrying a spear. But since its meaning was known, he was content with what had appeared of his speech, and did not state what was omitted from it. And they may say to a traveller when they bid him farewell: "accompanied, safe", omitting "go, and set out", since its meaning is known, even though its mention is dropped.

Likewise what is omitted from the saying of God, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, since by His saying, may He be mighty and exalted, ﴿You alone we worship﴾, what He meant by His saying ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ is known, namely the meaning of His command to His servants, and the indication of what appeared of the speech made the disclosure of what was omitted unnecessary.

We have already related the report we previously mentioned, from its beginning, in the interpretation of God's saying ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, from Ibn 'Abbas, and that he used to say: Gabriel said to Muhammad: "Say, O Muhammad: 'All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds'", and we explained that Gabriel only taught Muhammad what he was commanded to teach him. [In the printed edition: "fi tanzil qawl Allah" (in the revelation of God's saying).] See what has passed just now for hadith no. 151. And this report indicates the soundness of what we said in the interpretation of that.

* *

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Lord﴾.**

Abu Ja'far said: The explanation of the interpretation of the name of God which is "Allah", in "In the name of God", has already passed, so we have no need to repeat it in this place.

As for the interpretation of His saying ﴿Lord (rabb)﴾, the word rabb in the speech of the Arabs has various meanings: the lord who is obeyed among them is called a rabb, and of this is the saying of Labid ibn Rabi'a:

And on a day, He destroyed the lord of Kinda and his son, and the lord of Mudar, between Khabt and 'Ar'ar.

[His Diwan, qasida 15/32. The lord of Kinda was Hujr, the father of Imru' al-Qays. The lord of Mudar: Hudhayfa ibn Badr, as the commentator of his Diwan says, but I am in doubt about it, for Hudhayfa ibn Badr was killed at al-Haba'a. Labid mentions Khabt and 'Ar'ar, and they are two other places.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 2 (part 2 of 2):

He means by *rabb Kinda* (رَبِّ كِندة): the lord (sayyid) of Kinda. From this is the saying of Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan:

*You hasten toward al-Nu'man until you reach him,*
*ransom for you from a lord (rabb), my new wealth and my old.* [[Diwanuhu: 89; al-Mukhassas 7: 154. al-Tarif and al-Tarif (طريف): newly acquired wealth, the opposite of al-talid and al-talid (تالد), which is the ancient wealth inherited with you.]]

A man who sets right a thing is called *rabb* (ربّ). From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq ibn Ghalib:

*They were like a foolish woman who, when she poured her ghee (salaʾ) into a hide that had not been treated (marbub),* [[Diwanuhu: 25. Salaʾa al-samn (سلأ السمن) means he cooked and treated it, melting its cream. al-Salaʾ, with a kasra on the sin, is ghee. Haqana al-laban fi al-wat'b and al-ma' fi al-siqaʾ means he confined it in it and filled it. Rabba nahhi al-samn (ربّ نحى السمن) means he greased it with rabb, which is the molasses of every fruit; they used to grease the leather of the jar with rabb until they sealed and made it right, so its smell became good and the ghee was prevented from seeping, without spoiling its taste or smell. If they did not do this to the jar, the ghee spoiled. Adim marbub: a hide that has been made right with rabb. He says: they did what this foolish woman did, and what they had labored to manage and make was spoiled.]]

He means by that: in a hide that was not made right. From this it is said: "So-and-so *yarubbu* his favour (sani'atahu) with so-and-so," when he tries to set it right and keep it lasting. From this is the saying of Alqama ibn Abada:

*You were a man to whom my affairs (rababati) came, and before you those (rabbatni) managed me, so I was lost, the lords (rubub).* [[Diwanuhu: 29; it comes in the tafsir of the verse of Surat Al 'Imran: 79 (3: 233, Bulaq edition); al-Mukhassas 17: 154. The poet says it to al-Harith ibn Abi Shamir al-Ghassani, king of Ghassan, who is the well-known al-Harith al-A'raj. Ibn Sida said: "Rubub is the plural of rabb, meaning: the kings who were before you wasted my affair, and now my rababa has come to you, that is, the management of my affair and its setting right. So rabb here means master (malik), as if he said: those who used to rule my affair before you wasted it." Al-Tabari said later: "He means by his saying 'rabbatni': those who had authority over my affair and were responsible for it before you, who would manage it and set it right, but they did not set it right; rather they wasted me, so I was lost." Al-Rababa: kingdom, and it is also the covenant and the pact. With this meaning the verse was interpreted, and they supported it with the variant of those who related "amanati" (my trust) in place of "rababati." The first is better.]]

He means by his saying "afdat ilayka" (it came to you): my rababa reached you, so you became the one who manages my affair and sets it right, when I came out from the rababa of another than you among the kings who were before you over me [[In the printed edition: "min al-muluk alladhina kanu" (from the kings who were); they changed it to match the phrasing they were accustomed to.]], and they wasted my affair and left off attending to it. They are the *rubub* (ربوب), whose singular is *rabb* (ربّ). The one who owns a thing is called its *rabb* (ربّه). The meaning of *al-rabb* (الربّ) may also vary in other aspects besides these, but they all return to some of these three aspects.

So our Lord, may His majesty be exalted, is: the Master (sayyid) to whom there is no like, and no equal in His lordship; the one who sets right the affairs of His creation with the blessings He has bestowed upon them; and the Owner to whom belong creation and command.

And in accordance with what we have said in interpreting His words, may His majesty be exalted, *﴿Lord of the worlds﴾*, there came a report from Ibn Abbas:
