**155** – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara related to us, saying: Abu Rawq related to us, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Jibril said to Muhammad: "O Muhammad, say: *﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾*." Ibn Abbas said: He says: Say, "All praise is for Allah, to whom belongs all creation: the seven heavens and whoever is in them, and the earths all of them and whoever is in them, and what is between them, of what is known and what is not known." He says: know, O Muhammad, that your Lord this, nothing resembles Him. [[Report 155: The weakness of this chain was discussed in detail earlier, under number 137. This report is in Ibn Kathir 1: 44, al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 13, and al-Shawkani 1: 11. The last two also attribute it to Ibn Abi Hatim. In the printed edition and in Ibn Kathir: "wa al-ard wa man fihinna" (and the earth and whoever is in it).]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words: *﴿al-'alamin﴾* (الْعَالَمِينَ).

Abu Ja'far said: *al-'alamun* (العالَمون) is the plural of *'alam* (عالَم), and *'alam* is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like *al-anam* (the creatures), *al-rahat* (the men), *al-jaysh* (the army), and similar nouns that are coined for a collective with no singular from their own form.

*Al-'alam* is a name for the kinds of nations, and each kind of them is an *'alam*. The people of each generation of each kind are the *'alam* of that generation and that time. So mankind is an *'alam*, and each people of a time among them is the *'alam* of that time. The jinn are an *'alam*, and likewise all the kinds of creation: each kind of them is the *'alam* of its time. For this reason it was pluralized and said *'alamun*, and its singular is a collective, because the *'alam* of each time of those is the *'alam* of that time. From this is the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

*So Khindif is the chief of this 'alam.* [[Diwanuhu: 60; Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara': 64. Khindif: the mother of the Banu Ilyas ibn Mudar, Mudrika and Tabikha, from whom the great foundations of the Arabs branched out.]]

So he made them the *'alam* of his time. This view that we have stated is the view of Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it is the meaning of the saying of the majority of the exegetes.

**156** – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara related to us, saying: Abu Rawq related to us, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas: *﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾*: All praise is for Allah, to whom belongs all creation: the heavens and the earths and whoever is in them, and what is between them, of what is known and not known. [[Report 156: It is an abridgement of the preceding one, 155.]]

**157** – And Muhammad ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from Shabib, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: *﴿Lord of the worlds﴾*: the jinn and mankind. [[Report 157: A sound chain. Muhammad ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz, the teacher of al-Tabari: they spoke about him because of one hadith. The truth is that there is no harm in him, as al-Daraqutni said. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, and has a good biography in Tarikh Baghdad 5: 343–346. Abu 'Asim: he is al-Nabil, al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad, the memorizer and proof. Shabib: he is Ibn Bishr al-Bajali. Commentary on the words of Allah: ﴿Ar-Rahmani r-Rahim﴾ (The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful).

Abu Ja'far said: The explanation of the meaning of His words ﴿Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim﴾ has already been given in the explanation of ﴿Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim﴾, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it in this place.

We did not need to clarify the reason for repeating it in this place, since we do not regard "Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim" as a verse of the Opening Chapter (al-Fatihah). Otherwise a questioner could ask: what is the purpose of repeating it in this place, when Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has already described Himself with it in His words "Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim", especially given how close one verse is to the other and their adjacency to each other? Rather, this is for us a proof against the error of those who claim that "Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim" is a verse of the Opening Chapter. For if that were so, it would mean repeating a verse with one meaning and one wording twice, with no separation between them. Nothing in the Book of Allah contains two adjacent verses repeated with the same wording and the same meaning, without a separation of speech whose meaning differs from theirs. Rather, a verse is repeated in full within a single chapter only with breaks separating the repetitions and with speech interposed that alters the meaning of the repeated verses or their wording. There is no separator between the words of Allah, blessed and exalted is His name, "Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim" in "Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim", and the words of Allah: "Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim", in "Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin".

If someone says: But "Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin" is a separator between them.

It is said: A group of the scholars of interpretation (ta'wil) have rejected that, and said: this is of the postponed (mu'akhkhar) that has the meaning of the preposed (muqaddam). The actual text is: "Al-hamdu lillahi ar-Rahmani r-Rahim rabbi l-'alamin, maliki yawmi d-din" (Praise be to Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, Lord of the worlds, Master of the Day of Judgment). They cited as evidence for their claim His words "Master of the Day of Judgment", saying: Allah's words "Maliki yawmi d-din" are a teaching from Allah to His servant to describe Him with sovereignty (al-mulk) in the reading of one who reads "Maliki" (with a short vowel), and with ownership (al-milk) in the reading of one who reads "Maliki" (as "Malik"). They said: what is more fitting to be adjacent to His description with sovereignty or ownership is what is similar to that description, and that is His words "Lord of the worlds", which is a report of His possession of all kinds of creation; and that what is adjacent to His description with greatness and divinity should be what is similar to it in meaning of praise of Him, and that is His words "Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim".

They claimed that this is for them evidence that His words "Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim" have the meaning of being placed before "Rabb al-'alamin", even though apparently it comes after it. They said: examples of this, of the preposed that has the meaning of the postponed, and of the postponed that has the meaning of the preposed, are far more widespread in the speech of the Arabs and more numerous in their usage than can be counted. Among them is the verse of Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah:

"The phantom visited — and where is it from you? — briefly, so return to your visitor with peace, a greeting."

meaning: the phantom visited briefly, and where is it from you? Just as He, mighty is His praise, said in His Book: ﴿Al-hamdu lillahi lladhi anzala 'ala 'abdihi l-kitaba wa lam yaj'al lahu 'iwajan, qayyiman﴾ (Praise be to Allah, who sent down the Book to His servant and did not place in it any crookedness, but made it straight) [Surah al-Kahf: 1], meaning: Praise be to Allah who sent down the Book to His servant, straight, and did not make crookedness in it, and similar to that. In this there is a clear proof for the correctness of the view of those who deny that ﴿Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim﴾ is a verse of the Opening Chapter.

[Thus Abu Ja'far, may Allah have mercy on him, held that "Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim" is not a verse of al-Fatihah, and argued for his position with what you see. This is not the place to expand on the disagreement or to demonstrate the view opposed to what Ibn Jarir said.

I have investigated this question and set out, in my own judgment and understanding, the sound proofs that it is a verse of al-Fatihah, in my commentary on Sunan al-Tirmidhi, vol. 2, pp. 16–25, and the reference to it here is sufficient. Ahmad Muhammad Shakir.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The reciters differ in their recitation of ﴿Malik yawm al-din﴾. Some of them recite it as "Malik yawm al-din" (King of the Day of Judgment), some recite it as ﴿Maliki yawm al-din﴾, and some recite it as ﴿Malika yawm al-din﴾ with the kaf in the accusative. We have thoroughly examined the transmitted reports of those from whom readings were narrated concerning this in our book "Kitab al-Qira'at" (the Book of Readings), and we have informed (the reader) of the reading we choose there, and the reason that makes the reading we have chosen correct. We disliked repeating that here, since our aim in this book is to explain the aspects of the interpretation (ta'wil) of the verses of the Qur'an, not the aspects of their recitation.

There is no disagreement among all the people of knowledge of the Arabic language that al-Malik (the King) is derived from al-mulk (sovereignty), and that al-malik (the Owner/Master) is derived from al-milk (ownership). So the interpretation of the reading of one who reads ﴿Maliki yawm al-din﴾ is that sovereignty belongs to God alone on the Day of Judgment, exclusively, over all His creation, those who in the previous life in this world were tyrannical kings contending with Him for sovereignty and vying with Him for exclusive possession of pride, greatness, authority and compulsion (al-jabriyya) [[al-Jabriyya and al-Jabarut are one and the same, and it is one of the attributes of God the Exalted. Al-Jabbar: the Subduer above His servants, who subdues them to what He wills of command and prohibition, glorified and exalted be He.]]. On the Day of Judgment, when they meet God, they will be certain that they are the humbled and abased [[al-Saghara is the plural of saghir: one who accepts humiliation and acknowledges it. Al-Adhilla is the plural of dhalil.]], and that sovereignty, pride, might and splendour belong to Him—beyond them and beyond others. As He, mighty is His remembrance and sanctified are His names, said in His revelation: ﴿The Day when they will come forth, nothing of them will be hidden from God. "Whose is the sovereignty today?" "God's, the One, the Subduer."﴾ [Surah Ghafir: 16]. Thus He, exalted is His remembrance, informs that He alone will possess sovereignty on that day, not the kings of this world, who will have passed from their sovereignty on the Day of Judgment into humiliation and abasement, and from their worldly life into loss in the Hereafter.

As for the interpretation of the reading of one who reads ﴿Maliki yawm al-din﴾, it is what has been reported to us:

166 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Bishr ibn 'Umara, who said: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from Abdullah ibn Abbas: ﴿Malik yawm al-din﴾, he said: No one on that day will possess any command with Him as they possessed in the world. Then he said: ﴿They will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and who speaks correctly﴾ [Surah al-Naba: 38], and he said: ﴿And the voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful﴾ [Surah Ta-Ha: 108]. And he said: ﴿And they will not intercede except for whom He approves﴾ [[The report 166, the weakness of its chain was discussed in detail earlier at 137. This report, together with what follows at 167, was transmitted by Ibn Kathir (1:46) without chain or attribution, and al-Suyuti (1:14) transmitted it and attributed it also to Ibn Abi Hatim. Ibn Kathir said: "Others among the Companions, the Successors and the early scholars said likewise, and it is apparent."]] [Surah al-Anbiya: 28].

Abu Ja'far said: The more appropriate of the two interpretations for the verse, and the more correct of the two readings in recitation in my view, is the first interpretation, which is the reading of one who reads "Maliki," in the sense of "al-mulk" (sovereignty). For affirming to Him exclusive sovereignty implies His exclusive ownership, and the excellence of the king's (malik) rank over the owner (malik) [[In the manuscript: "al-mulk 'ala al-milk", and they are the same.]], since it is known that there is no king except that he is also an owner, while an owner may not be a king.

Furthermore, God, mighty is His remembrance, has informed His servants in the verse before His words ﴿Malik yawm al-din﴾ that He is the owner of all the worlds, their lord, their guardian, the one who looks after them, and merciful to them in this world and the Hereafter, by His words: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾.

Since He, mighty is His remembrance, has informed them of His ownership of them in this way by His words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, the most fitting of His attributes to follow that is what the words ﴿Lord of the worlds, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ do not contain, despite the closeness between the two verses in their connection and proximity, since His wisdom is a wisdom unlike any other wisdom. And in repeating His description, mighty is His remembrance, as ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, there would be a repetition of what has already passed of His description in His words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, despite the nearness of the two verses and the closeness of the two attributes. In such repetition there would be a repeating of different words with agreeing meanings, which would not give the hearer of what is repeated any benefit that he needs. What His attributes mighty is His remembrance do not contain before the words ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ is the meaning in His words ﴿King of the Day of Judgment﴾, namely His description as the King.

It is therefore clear that the more correct of the two readings and the more worthy of the two interpretations for the Book is the reading of one who reads ﴿Malik yawm al-din﴾, in the sense of exclusively affirming sovereignty to Him on the Day of Judgment, rather than the reading of one who reads ﴿Malik yawm al-din﴾ in the sense that He possesses judgment among them and the decisive verdict, alone, to the exclusion of all His creation.

If someone supposes that His words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ are a report about His sovereignty over them in this world and not the Hereafter, and that this requires connecting it, by a report about Himself, with the statement that He is the one who possesses them in the Hereafter in the manner of His possession of them in this world, by His words ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾—then he has been heedless and has erred [[The verb "aghfala" is intransitive, not transitive. Its meaning: he entered into heedlessness and forgetfulness and fell into them. It is an Arabic usage that is attested, though not found in the dictionaries, and it is like their saying "anjada" (he entered Najd), and similar forms. It suffices as proof of its Arabic status that it is the language of al-Shafi'i, who used it more often in al-Risala and al-Umm. Among that is his saying in al-Risala, p. 42, no. 136: "And by taqlid, whoever among them has been heedless has been heedless."]].

That is because if it were permissible for someone to suppose that His words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ are restricted in meaning to a report about the lordship over the world of this life, to the exclusion of the world of the Hereafter, without any indication that this is the meaning in the apparent revelation, or in a report from the Messenger ﷺ transmitted about it, or in an existing proof of reason, then it would be permissible for another to suppose that this is restricted to the world of the time in which the words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ were revealed, to the exclusion of all that comes after it of worlds in the times that follow. For it is correct, by what we have already explained, that the world of each time is other than the world of the time that follows it.

If someone is dull and fails to know the correctness of this by what we have already mentioned, then in the saying of God, exalted is His praise: ﴿And We gave the Children of Israel the Book, and wisdom, and prophethood, and provided them with good things, and preferred them over the worlds﴾ [Surah al-Jathiya: 16], there is a clear proof that the world of each time is other than the world of the time before it and the world of the time after it, since God, exalted is His praise, preferred the community of our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ over all the earlier nations, and informed them of that in His words: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 110]. It is therefore known from this that the Children of Israel in the age of our Prophet, despite their denial of him ﷺ, were not the best of the worlds; rather, the best of the worlds in that age and after it until the Hour is established were the believers in him who followed his path, apart from those others among the nations who denied and strayed from his path.

Since the fallacy of an interpreter is evident who interprets His words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ as meaning that God is the Lord of the worlds of the time of our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ alone, to the exclusion of the worlds of all other times, it is equally evident that the claim of one who asserts that its interpretation is: Lord of the world of this life, to the exclusion of the world of the Hereafter, and that ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ is connected to it so that it may be known that in the Hereafter He possesses them and lordship over them in the same way as in this world—is false.

And the one who makes this claim should be asked to explain the difference between himself and another who makes the same arbitrary claim about the interpretation of His words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, who arbitrarily says that He only means by it that He is the Lord of the worlds of the time of Muhammad ﷺ, to the exclusion of the worlds of other times, past before him and occurring after him, just as the speaker of this statement claimed that He meant by it the worlds of this life to the exclusion of the worlds of the Hereafter—whether from a principle or an indication [[The sentence reads: "And the one who makes this claim should be asked the difference . . . from a principle or an indication", and there is a gap between them.]]. Whatever he says about one of them, he will be obliged to say the same about the other.

As for one who claims that the interpretation of His words ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ is that He is the One who possesses the establishment of the Day of Judgment, the objection we raised against the previous speaker applies equally to him. For the establishment of the Resurrection is only the restoration of creatures who have perished to the forms they had before destruction, in the abode in which God has prepared for them what He has prepared. And they are the worlds (al-'alamun) concerning whom He, mighty is His remembrance, has informed that He is their Lord in His words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.

As for the interpretation of this in the reading of one who reads ﴿Malika yawm al-din﴾, he intended: O Master of the Day of Judgment, and he put it in the accusative by way of intending the vocative and invocation, as He, mighty is His praise, said: ﴿Joseph, turn away from this﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 29], meaning: O Joseph, turn away from this. And as the poet of the Banu Asad said—a verse which is said to be pre-Islamic:

"If you have falsely accused me of it, O Juz',
then you will soon meet its like."

[[The poet is a Jahili Mukhadram, Hadrami ibn 'Amir al-Asadi, who came as a delegation to the Messenger of God ﷺ with a group of the Banu Asad, and they all embraced Islam. The reason for his saying this verse: his brothers were nine, and they sat by a well and were swallowed up by it, and he inherited from them. His cousin Juz' ibn Malik ibn Majma' envied him and said to him: Who is like you? Your brothers died and you inherited from them, and you have become comfortable and prosperous. Not long after, Juz' and nine of his brothers sat by a well, it swallowed up his brothers, and he escaped. When this reached Hadrami he said: "Surely to God we belong and to Him we return," a phrase that matched a decree and left a grudge, meaning his saying to Juz': "then you will meet its like soon." "Azananahu bi shay'" means he accused him of it. See al-Qali's Amali 1:67, al-Kamil 1:41–42 and others.]]

He means: O Juz'. And as the other said:

"You have lied, by the House of God, you will not marry them,
O sons of the Shabb whose two plaits are milked and squeezed."

[[It is attributed in Lisan (qrn) and Majaz al-Qur'an (100) to a man of the Banu Asad, and the verse is in Sibawayh 1:295 / 2:7, 65, and it is a well-known evidence. "Banu Shabb qarnaha" means a people; he says: sons of the one called Shabb qarnaha, i.e., O sons of the old woman who grazes, who has no concern except to tighten the sirar (cord) on the udder until the milk gathers, then she is milked. That is a reproach to her. Al-Qarn: the braid.]]

He means: O sons of Shabb Qarnaha. It was only the interpretation of reading it in the accusative, "Malika" with the kaf, in the sense I have described, that confused him in directing His words ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ with the direction, given the genitive and the lowering of ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾. He thought that the meaning of that is not sound after taking ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ as genitive, so he put "Malika yawm al-din" in the accusative, so that ﴿iyyaka na'budu﴾ would be an address to Him. As if he meant: O Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help. And if he had known the interpretation of the beginning of the sura, and that "Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds" is a command from God to His servant to say it—as we mentioned earlier from the report from Ibn Abbas that Gabriel said to the Prophet ﷺ on behalf of God, mighty is His remembrance: Say, O Muhammad, ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, and say also, O Muhammad: ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾ [[See: 151, 155.]]—and if he had understood from the Arabs that it is their custom, when they relate or command the relating of a report that follows a speech, to address and then speak about an absent party, and to speak about an absent party and then return to address, because in relating by speech there is the sense of the absent and the present, as when they say to a man: "I said to your brother: If you stood, I would stand," and "I said to your brother: If he stood, I would stand"—then the way out of what he found difficult, in directing "Malik yawm al-din" in the genitive, would have been easy for him.

As an example of "Malik yawm al-din" in the genitive, followed by a return to address with "iyyaka na'budu," as we mentioned before, is the well-known verse from the poetry of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

"Alas for my soul! Where has the freshness of Khalid gone,
and the whiteness of your face for the dusty ground?"

[[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 2:101. In the printed edition: "jildat," which is an error; "jidda" means his new youth. "Jidda" is the opposite of decay. "Al-turab al-a'far": the white, rarely trodden by people because of its barrenness. Khalid: a friend of his from his tribe, whom he mourns.]]

He returned to address with his words "and the whiteness of your face", after the report about Khalid had passed in the sense of a report about an absent party.

And from it is the saying of Labid ibn Rabi'a:

"The soul has spent the night complaining to me, distressed,
and I have carried you seven, after seventy."

[[The second part of his Diwan: 46. Ibn Sallam said in Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara' (p. 50), mentioning this verse and another with it, that they were transmitted from al-Sha'bi (Ibn Sa'd 6:178), and both are attributed to Labid; then he said: "There is no disagreement that this is fabricated, with which many narrations are multiplied, and which is used to keep awake at the courts of kings, and kings do not examine closely." "Ajhasha bil-bukka'": he prepared himself for it and his crying choked him.]]

He returned to addressing his own soul, though the report about it had been given in the form of a report about an absent party.

And from it is the saying of God, who is the truest speech and the most established proof: ﴿Until when you are in the ship, and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ [Surah Yunus: 22], where He addressed and then returned to the report about the absent, and did not say "and sailed with you." The examples of this from poetry and Arabic speech are too many to count, and what we have mentioned is sufficient for one who is granted understanding of it.

Thus the reading "Malika yawm al-din" is forbidden and not permissible, since all the authoritative reciters and scholars of the Ummah are unanimous in rejecting the recitation with it.

On the interpretation of His words, mighty is His praise: ﴿yawm al-din﴾ (the Day of Judgment).

Abu Ja'far said: "Al-din" in this place, by interpretation, means the reckoning and the recompense for deeds, as Ka'b ibn Ju'ayl said:

"When they throw at us, we throw at them,
and we repay them just as they lend to us."

[[Al-Kamil of al-Mubarrad 1:191, Waq'at Siffin of Nasr ibn Muzahim 1:52, al-Mukhassas 17:155.]]

And as the other said:

"Know and be certain that your sovereignty is passing,
and know that as you repay, so you will be repaid."

[[Al-Kamil of al-Mubarrad 1:192, attributed to Yazid ibn Abi al-Sa'q al-Kilabi, and likewise in Jamharat al-Amthal of al-'Askari: 196, al-Mukhassas 17:155; and in Lisan (z-n-'a) and (d-y-n) attributed to Khuwaylid ibn Nawfal al-Kilabi, and in al-Khizana 4:230 to some of the Kilabis. They say that al-Harith ibn Abi Shamir al-Ghassani, whenever a woman from Qays 'Aylan pleased him, would send for her and seize her by force. He took the daughter of Yazid ibn al-Sa'q al-Kilabi, and her father was absent; when he returned he was informed. He went to him, stood before him and said: "O King who feeds!, do you not see the night and the morning, how they alternate? Can you bring the sun by night? Or do you have hands over the King?" "O Harith, be certain that your sovereignty is passing . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ."]]

He means: as you repay, so you will be repaid.

And from this is the saying of God, mighty is His praise: ﴿No indeed! Rather you deny the Din﴾—meaning: the recompense—﴿And indeed over you are guardians﴾ [Surah al-Infitar: 9-10], who count what you do of deeds, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then why, if you are not to be recompensed (ghayra madinin)﴾ [Surah al-Waqi'a: 86], meaning: not recompensed for your deeds and not called to account.

"Al-din" has meanings in Arabic speech other than the meaning of reckoning and recompense, which we will mention in their places, God willing.

In accordance with what we have said in the interpretation of His words ﴿yawm al-din﴾, reports have come from the early exegetes, together with the confirmation of the verses of poetry, which support their interpretation that they have given.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):

Then he said: ﴿Surely His is the creation and the command﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 54]. [[Report 167 - its takhrij has preceded in report 166.]]

He did not state the cause of his doubt regarding its chain, and despite his doubt he narrated through it extensively, but he never took it as a proof.

Nevertheless, I see it as a chain requiring careful investigation. The scholars of hadith have spoken about it and about some of its narrators. I have traced what they said and what its investigation calls for, as far as I was able, and an opinion has appeared to me in it which I hope is correct, God willing. My success is only through God:

As for al-Tabari's teacher, "Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani": I have found no biography of him, nor any mention of him in any of the references available to me, other than what al-Tabari also narrates from him in his History, which is more than fifty places in its first two volumes. There is no need for us to examine his biography in terms of jarh and ta'dil, since this Tafsir which he narrates from Amr ibn Hammad is well known among the people of knowledge of hadith. It is merely the narration of a book, not the narration of a specific hadith.

"Amr ibn Hammad": he is Amr ibn Hammad ibn Talhah al-Qannad, and he is sometimes ascribed to his grandfather, so he is called Amr ibn Talhah. He is trustworthy (thiqah). Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih. Ibn Sa'd included his biography in al-Tabaqat 6: 285 and said: "He was trustworthy, God willing." He died in the year 222. Ibn Abi Hatim included his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/1/228, and narrated from his father and from Yahya ibn Ma'in that they both said of him: "Saduq (truthful)."

Asbat ibn Nasr al-Hamdani: he is disputed. Ahmad declared him weak, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat: 410. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 1/2/53 and mentioned no criticism of him. Ibn Abi Hatim included his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/332 and narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in that he said: "Asbat ibn Nasr is trustworthy." We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad, in hadith 1286.

Isma'il ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Karimah al-Suddi: he is al-Suddi al-Kabir, a Qurashi by clientage (mawla), client of Zaynab bint Qays ibn Makhramah, of the Banu Abd Manaf, as al-Bukhari stated in his two histories: al-Saghir: 141-142, and al-Kabir 1/1/361. He was a Tabi'i who heard from Anas, as al-Bukhari also stated, and narrated from other Companions and from many Tabi'un. He is trustworthy. Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih. Ahmad ibn Hanbal authenticated him, as narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/184. He also narrated from Ahmad, who said: "Yahya ibn Ma'in once said to me in the presence of Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi: 'al-Suddi is weak.' Abd al-Rahman became angry and disliked what he had said." In al-Mizan and al-Tahdhib it is related that al-Sha'bi was told: "al-Suddi has been given a share of knowledge of the Qur'an," and he said: "He has been given a share of ignorance of the Qur'an!" I think this statement of al-Sha'bi may be the basis for the words of everyone who spoke against al-Suddi unjustly. For this reason al-Bukhari gave no weight to this statement of al-Sha'bi and did not narrate it; rather, he narrated in al-Kabir from Musaddad, from Yahya, who said: "I heard Ibn Abi Khalid say: al-Suddi is more knowledgeable of the Qur'an than al-Sha'bi." He also narrated in his histories from Ibn al-Madini, from Yahya - namely al-Qattan - who said: "I have not seen anyone mention al-Suddi except with good, and no one has abandoned him." In al-Tahdhib: "al-Ajli said: trustworthy, a scholar of tafsir and a narrator of it." We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad, 807. al-Suddi died in the year 127.

"al-Suddi": with a damma on the sin and a shadda on the dal, unpointed letters, a nisba to "al-Sudda," which is the doorway, because he used to sit at the portico (sudda) of the mosque in Kufa and sell headscarves there.

Abu Malik: he is al-Ghifari, whose name is Ghazwan. He is a trustworthy Kufan Tabi'i. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 4/1/108, Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat 6: 206, and Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/2/55, and Yahya ibn Ma'in's authentication of him was narrated.

Abu Salih: he is the client of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, whose name is Badham, and it is said Badhan. He is a trustworthy Tabi'i; we have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad, 2030. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 1/2/144 and narrated from Muhammad ibn Bashshar, who said: "Ibn Mahdi abandoned the hadith of Abu Salih." Likewise Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/431-432 from Ahmad ibn Hanbal from Ibn Mahdi. But he also narrated from Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan, who said: "I have not seen anyone among our companions abandon Abu Salih, the client of Umm Hani, and I have not heard anyone say anything about him; neither Shu'bah nor Za'idah nor Abd Allah ibn Uthman abandoned him." He also narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in, who said: "Abu Salih, the client of Umm Hani, is not objectionable. If al-Kalbi narrates from him, it is worthless; if other than al-Kalbi narrates from him, there is no objection in it, because al-Kalbi narrates it sometimes from his own opinion, sometimes from Abu Salih, and sometimes from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas." He means by this that the criticism of what is narrated from him concerns the narration of al-Kalbi, as is evident.

This is concerning the first part of this chain, for in reality it is two or three chains. The first of them is this one connected to Ibn Abbas.

The second part, or second chain: "and from Murrah al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud." The one who narrates from Murrah al-Hamdani is al-Suddi himself.

Murrah: he is Ibn Shurahil al-Hamdani al-Kufi, a trustworthy Tabi'i, one of the senior Tabi'un, about whom there is no disagreement among them.

The third part, or third chain: "and from people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ."

This also is a narration of al-Suddi himself from people among the Companions.

So al-Suddi narrates these tafsirs of verses of the Qur'an: from two Tabi'un from Ibn Abbas, and from one Tabi'i from Ibn Mas'ud, and by his own narration from people among the Companions.

The earlier scholars, the imams, have spoken about this tafsir with these chains, in a way that may give the impression that it was composed by someone other than al-Suddi among those who narrated from him, but I have now become certain that it is a book composed by al-Suddi.

Among that is the statement of Ibn Sa'd in the biography of "Amr ibn Hammad al-Qannad" 6: 285: "The companion of the tafsir of Asbat ibn Nasr from al-Suddi." He said in the biography of "Asbat ibn Nasr" 6: 261: "He was the narrator of al-Suddi, and narrated the tafsir from him." He said before that in the biography of "al-Suddi" 6: 225: "Isma'il ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, the author of the tafsir." He said before that also, in the biography of "Abu Malik al-Ghifari" 6: 206: "Abu Malik al-Ghifari, the companion of the tafsir, and he narrated little hadith."

But what gives preference to it being a book composed by al-Suddi, in which he gathered the tafsir through these three channels, is the statement of Ahmad ibn Hanbal in al-Tahdhib 1: 314, in the biography of al-Suddi: "He is good in hadith, except that this tafsir which he brings has been given a chain and he forced it." And the statement of the Hafiz in al-Tahdhib also 1: 315: "Al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and others have narrated the tafsir of al-Suddi in their tafsirs, scattered across the surahs, through the route of Asbat ibn Nasr from him."

And the statement of al-Suyuti in al-Itqan 2: 224, quoting al-Khalil in al-Irshad: "The tafsir of Isma'il al-Suddi, he brings it with chains to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. The imams narrated from al-Suddi, such as al-Thawri and Shu'bah. But the tafsir that he compiled was narrated by Asbat ibn Nasr, and they did not agree upon Asbat. Yet the most reliable of the tafsirs is the tafsir of al-Suddi." Al-Suyuti then said: "The tafsir of al-Suddi, which he indicated, Ibn Jarir quotes much from it, through the route of al-Suddi from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah from Ibn Mas'ud, and [from] people among the Companions. Thus. Ibn Abi Hatim did not quote anything from it, because he committed himself to bring out only the soundest of what was transmitted. Al-Hakim brings out from it in his Mustadrak some things and authenticates them, but only through the route of Murrah from Ibn Mas'ud and people, only, not through the first route. Ibn Kathir said: this chain, through which al-Suddi narrates things, contains strangeness."

The first thing we point out in these statements is the contradiction between the two statements of al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar and al-Suyuti, regarding whether Ibn Abi Hatim brought out the tafsir of al-Suddi scattered throughout his tafsir, as al-Tabari did, according to Ibn Hajar's report, and that he turned away from it, according to al-Suyuti's report. I cannot assert anything definitively in this matter, since I have not seen the tafsir of Ibn Abi Hatim. But I lean towards preferring Ibn Hajar's report, as he is more precise and careful in transmission than al-Suyuti.

Then al-Suyuti was correct in what he reported from al-Hakim. For he narrates part of this tafsir in the Mustadrak, with his chain, to Ahmad ibn Nasr: "Amr ibn Talhah al-Qannad narrated to us, Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and from people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ." Then he authenticates it according to the condition of Muslim, and al-Dhahabi agrees with him in his summary. Among that is in the Mustadrak 2: 258, 260, 273, 321.

And al-Hakim is correct in this, for Muslim narrated from all the men of this chain, from Amr ibn Hammad ibn Talhah al-Qannad to Murrah al-Hamdani. He did not narrate from Abu Salih Badham nor from Abu Malik al-Ghifari, in the first part of the chain through which al-Suddi narrated his tafsirs.

As for the words of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal about al-Suddi, "except that this tafsir which he brings has been given a chain and he forced it," he does not mean what might be understood from its apparent meaning: that he fabricated a chain with no basis; for if that were so, he would be, in his view, a liar and a fabricator of narrations. Rather, he means, in my view, and God knows best, that he gathered these tafsirs from his narration from these people: from Abu Malik and Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah from Ibn Mas'ud, and from people among the Companions; then he put them all in detail, on the verses in which some tafsir was reported from this one or that one or those, and made for all of them this one chain, and forced himself to bring them all through it in one manner.

I mean: he gathered the scattered parts of these tafsirs into one book, and placed at its beginning these chains, intending by them that what he narrated of tafsir in this book does not go beyond these chains. I can hardly conceive that he narrated every word of these tafsirs from all of them. Rather, it is a book composed on tafsir, referring in general, not in detail, to narration from these people.

What led people into this doubt is the dispersal of these tafsirs in their places, as in the practice of al-Tabari before us, and the practice of Ibn Abi Hatim as reported by al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, and the practice of al-Hakim in the Mustadrak. I nearly affirm that this dispersal is an error on their part, because it gives the reader the impression that every word of these tafsirs is narrated through all these chains, since they bring them in full at every chain, while al-Hakim selects one chain which he mentions at each tafsir he wishes to narrate. What al-Hakim narrated, for instance, through the chain to Ibn Mas'ud, may not be something al-Suddi narrated explicitly from Ibn Mas'ud; perhaps it is from what he narrated from Ibn Abbas, or from what people among the Companions narrated, he having narrated something from each of them, so he attributed the whole to one chain without attributing the details.

Al-Suddi was not unique in this, and this is not a flaw or a defect in him. He intends to trace these tafsirs back to the Companions, some from Ibn Abbas, some from Ibn Mas'ud, and some from others among them. Other hadith transmitters and imams have done something similar, and that was not a criticism of them; rather, the later hafiz scholars accepted these works and included them in their collections. Yahudh...

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is His praise: ﴿Only You do we worship﴾.**

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of His saying ﴿Only You do we worship﴾ is: "To You, O Allah, we humble ourselves, we abase ourselves, and we submit, acknowledging You, O our Lord, in lordship, and not to anyone other than You."

171. As Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, he said: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to us, he said: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, who said: Jibril said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "Say, O Muhammad: ﴿Only You do we worship﴾," meaning: "Only You do we declare as one, and we fear and hope, O our Lord, not any other than You." [[The report 171: its chain is weak; we explained this in no. 137. This report and the one after it, 172, were gathered by al-Suyuti (1:14), and he also attributed them to Ibn Abi Hatim.]]

This is in agreement with the meaning of what we have said, from Ibn 'Abbas. We chose to explain its interpretation as meaning "we humble ourselves, abase ourselves, and submit," rather than explaining it as meaning "we hope and fear," even though hope and fear only exist together with humility. This is because "ʿubūdiyya" (servitude, worship), according to all the Arabs, originally means humility. They call a road that has been made smooth, which feet have trodden and travellers have levelled, "muʿabbad" (paved, made smooth). Among this is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-ʿAbd:

*She races noble, swift she-camels, and follows with a hoof, hoof upon a smoothed path.* [[Diwan of the Six Pre-Islamic Poets: 31. He describes his she-camel. "Tubari" means she races them and competes with them. "ʿItaq" is the plural of ʿatiq: noble, of pure lineage. "Nājiyāt" means swift in travel, from al-naja', speed of travel. "Waẓīf" is, on a camel's forelegs, the part from the wrist to the knee, and on its hind legs from the hock to the fetlock. Here by waẓīf he means the sole of the foot.]]

By "mawr" he means the road, and by "muʿabbad" the levelled and trodden. From this it is said of a camel tamed by riding for needs: "muʿabbad." And from it the slave is named "ʿabd" (slave) because of his humility before his master. The evidence for this from the poetry and speech of the Arabs is more than can be counted, and what we have mentioned is sufficient for one who is granted understanding of it, if Allah wills.

**The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And only You do we ask for help﴾.**

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of His saying ﴿And only You do we ask for help﴾ is: "And only You, our Lord, do we ask for help in our worship of You, in our obedience to You, and in all our affairs, not anyone besides You. For the one who disbelieves in You seeks help in his affairs from the object of his worship, the idols he worships apart from You. As for us, we seek help through You in all our affairs, sincerely devoting worship to You."

172. As the report narrated to us by Abu Kurayb, he said: Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, he said: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to me, he said: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And only You do we ask for help﴾, he said: "Only You do we ask for help in Your obedience and in all our affairs." [[Report 172: it has the same weak chain as the one before it, and we pointed to it there.]]

If someone says: What is the meaning of Allah commanding His servants to ask Him for help in His obedience? Is it permissible, when He has commanded them to obey Him, that He would not help them in it? Or would a speaker say to his Lord, "Only You do we ask for help in Your obedience," without already being helped in that statement, and that statement itself being obedience? So what is the point of a servant asking his Lord for what He has already given him?

It is said: The interpretation of that is other than the way you have taken. Rather, the believer who calls upon his Lord to help him in obeying Him is asking Him to help him in what remains of his life with what He has obligated upon him of obedience, not for what has already passed and gone of his righteous deeds in the time that has elapsed of his life. The servant's asking his Lord for that is permissible, because Allah's giving His servant that, together with empowering his limbs to perform what He has obligated upon him of obedience and imposed upon him of obligations, is a favour from Him, exalted is His praise, which He bestowed upon him, and a kindness from Him which He showed him. There is no corruption in management, nor injustice in judgment, in His leaving the bestowal of success to some of His servants while his servant is occupied with disobedience to Him and has turned away from His love, nor in His extending His favour to some of them while they strive hard in His love and hasten to His obedience. So it is not permissible for an ignorant person to be unaware of the place of Allah's judgment in commanding His servant to ask Him for help in obedience. [[In the printed edition: "the judgment of Allah and His command to His servant"; in the manuscript: "the judgment of Allah, His command" without the waw. What we have written is more correct. Al-ḥukm here means wisdom, as has been mentioned many times.]]

And in Allah's command, exalted is His praise, to His servants to say ﴿Only You do we worship and only You do we ask for help﴾, with the meaning of their asking Him for help in worship, is the clearest proof of the falsity of the view of those who hold the doctrine of delegation (tafwīd) among the people of qadar [[The people of qadar are the deniers of qadar, not its affirmers. Those who say delegation are the Qadariyya, the Mu'tazila and the Imamiyya. They claim that the matter has been delegated (i.e., returned) to man, so that his will is sufficient for bringing about his act, whether it be obedience or disobedience, and he is the creator of his actions, and choice is in his hand.]], who deny that Allah would command any of His servants with a command, or obligate him with the performance of a deed, except after giving him help in doing it and in abstaining from it. If what they say were as they say, the desire for Allah's help in His obedience would be void. For in their view, together with the existence of command, prohibition and obligation, it would be a binding right upon Allah to give the servant help in it, whether his servant asked Him or left off asking. Rather, in their view, His withholding that from him is injustice. And if the matter were as they say, the one who says ﴿Only You do we worship and only You do we ask for help﴾ would be asking his Lord only that He not be unjust.

And in the consensus of all the people of Islam, on the correctness of the speaker's saying, "O Allah, we ask You for help," and their error in the saying of the speaker, "O Allah, do not be unjust to us," there is a clear proof of the error of what those whose view I have described have said. For the interpretation of the speaker's words, in their view, is: "O Allah, we ask You for help—O Allah, do not withhold our help, for Your withholding it would be injustice from You."

If someone says: How is it said ﴿Only You do we worship and only You do we ask for help﴾, when the report about worship is put first, and the request for help in it is put after it? Indeed, worship only occurs with help, so the request for help should have been put forward before what is helped in, namely the act and worship?

It is said: Since it is known that there is no way for the servant to worship except with help from Allah, exalted is His praise, and since it is impossible for the servant to be a worshipper without being helped in worship, and to be helped in worship without actually performing it, then putting either of them forward over the other is equal. Just as it is equal when you say to a man, when he has fulfilled your need and treated you well in fulfilling it: "You fulfilled my need and treated me well," so you put the mention of his fulfilling your need first; or you say: "You treated me well and fulfilled my need," so you put the mention of the good treatment before the mention of fulfilling the need. For he is not fulfilling your need without being good to you, and he is not good to you without fulfilling your need. Likewise, it is equal whether the speaker says: "O Allah, we worship only You, so help us in Your worship," or says: "O Allah, help us in Your worship, for we worship only You."

Abu Ja'far said: Some of the heedless have thought that this is an instance of "the preposed that is meant to be postponed" (al-muqaddam alladhi maʿnāhu al-taʾkhīr), as Imru' al-Qays said:

*And if what I strive for of a meagre livelihood sufficed me, and I did not seek, a little of wealth [would suffice].* [[His Diwan 1:71.]]

He means by this: "A little wealth would suffice me, and I would not seek much." But that—regarding the meaning of preposing and postponing and the resemblance to Imru' al-Qays's verse—is far from the point. This is because a little wealth may suffice a man while he still seeks much; so the existence of what suffices him does not necessitate his abandoning the seeking of much. Thus it is not like worship, where its existence brings about the existence of help in it, and the existence of help in it brings about its existence. Therefore, the mention of one of them would indicate the other, and in the soundness of the speech, putting forward whichever of them is put forward before its counterpart would be balanced, placed in its rank and ordered in its position.

If someone says: What is the wisdom in repeating "iyyāka" (You) with "nastaʿīn" (we ask for help), when it has already been mentioned before "naʿbud" (we worship)? Why not say: "Only You do we worship and ask for help," since the one spoken of as the one worshipped is the same as the one spoken of as the one asked for help?

It is said to him: The kāf that is with "iyyā" is the kāf that would have joined the verb—I mean the verb "naʿbud"—had it been placed after the verb. It is the pronoun of the addressed person in the accusative object of the verb, so it was given a fuller form by "iyyā" placed in front, since nouns, when they stand alone by themselves, do not occur in the speech of the Arabs as a single letter.

Since the kāf of "iyyāka" is the pronoun of the addressed person, which would be a kāf alone joined to the verb if it came after the verb, and since its proper place is to be repeated with every verb it is joined to—so it is said: "O Allah, we worship You, we ask You for help, we praise You and we thank You"—and this is more eloquent in the speech of the Arabs than saying: "O Allah, we worship You and ask for help and praise," then likewise, when the pronoun of the addressed person is placed before the verb attached to "iyyā," the more eloquent is to repeat it with every verb. Just as the more eloquent speech is to repeat it with every verb when it comes after the verb and is joined to it, even though leaving out the repetition is permissible.

Some who have not examined carefully [[In the printed edition: "did not look carefully" (lam yumʿin al-naẓar); they changed it, as they did in p. 55, note 3.]] have thought that the repetition of "iyyāka" with "nastaʿīn," after it was already put forward in "iyyāka nastaʿīn," is in the sense of the saying of ʿAdi ibn Zayd al-ʿIbadi:

*And the one who made the sun a clear boundary, with no concealment, between the day and the night, separating them.* [[In Lisan al-ʿArab (under m-ṣ-r), attributed to Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt; Ibn Barri corrected it and attributed it to ʿAdi ibn Zayd. "Miṣr" means a barrier and a limit between two things. He says: He made the sun a limit and a sign between the night and the day.]]

And like the saying of Aʿshā Hamdan:

*Between al-Ashajj and Qays is a lofty one—bakh bakh for his father and for the newborn!* [[Diwan al-Aʿshayin: 323; al-Aghani 6:46, 61. Aʿshā Hamdan is ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Hamdani, Abu Mus'hib, who was one of the jurists and reciters; then he left that and composed poetry. He praised ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Ash'ath ibn Qays al-Kindi, who had rebelled against al-Hajjaj, and the jurists and reciters went out with him. When al-Hajjaj captured Aʿshā, he said to him, "Are you not the one who said:" and recited to him the verse—"By Allah, you will never boast again after this!" and he killed him. Al-Ashajj is al-Ash'ath, father of ʿAbd al-Rahman, and Qays is his grandfather. "Bakh bakh" is an expression of glorification and exaltation. This verse and the one before it are two pieces of evidence for the correctness of repeating "bayn" (between) with a non-attached pronoun; and similar examples are many. The people of our age err in those who say it, and they are in the error of mistake.]]

This is ignorance on the part of the one who says it, because the proper place of "iyyāka" is to be repeated with every verb, for the reason we described just above. The rule of "bayn" is not like this, for it, when it requires two, can only be repeated when it is repeated, since it cannot stand alone with one. And if it were used alone with one of the two nouns, in the case where it requires two, the speech would be almost impossible. That is because if someone said, "The sun has separated between the day," his speech would be a *khalf* (a faulty utterance), because it falls short of what is needed, from the completion that "bayn" requires.

And if someone said, "O Allah, *iyyāka naʿbud*," that would be a complete utterance. So it became known from this that the need of every word that is like "iyyāka naʿbud" for "iyyāka" is the same as the need of "naʿbud" for it, and that the correct thing is for "iyyāka" to be with it, since each word in it is a complete predicative sentence of a subject and predicate. And the clear ruling is that the opposite of this is like the ruling of "bayn" in what we mentioned, where the two are joined together, of which we have described the statement.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Guide us﴾.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The meaning of His words ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ in this place, according to us, is: "Grant us success (tawfiq) in steadfastness upon it," as has been related from Ibn 'Abbas:

173 - Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Ammara related to us, saying: Abu Rawq related to us, from al-Dahhak, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, who said: Jibril said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "Say, O Muhammad: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾." He means: "Inspire us with the guiding way." [[It will come in full with its takhrij under no. 179.]]

And His inspiring them with that is His granting them success, as we have said in its interpretation. Its meaning is similar to the meaning of His words ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, in that it is the servant's request of his Lord for success in steadfastness in acting in obedience to Him, and in reaching the truth and the correct course in what He has commanded him and forbidden him, concerning what he will face of his life, not what has already passed of his deeds and been concluded in the past of his life. Just as in His words ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾, it is a request from him to his Lord for assistance in performing the obedience He has imposed upon him in what remains of his life.

So the meaning of the statement is: "O Allah, You alone we worship, with no partner for You, sincerely devoting worship to You apart from whatever else is worshipped, of gods and idols. So help us in Your worship, and grant us success in what You granted success to those upon whom You bestowed favour, of Your prophets and the people of Your obedience, of the path and the method."

If someone says: "From where did you find guidance in the speech of the Arabs to mean success (tawfiq)?"

It is said to him: That is in their speech more frequent and more apparent than the number of the evidences that have come from them on that cannot be counted. Among that is the saying of the poet:

"Let not Allah, who guides you, deprive me of my request,
and let me not be like one whom travel has destroyed."

He means by it: "May Allah grant you success in fulfilling my need." And among it is the saying of another:

"And let not the Sovereign King, who guides you, hasten me,
for every station has its speech."

It is known that he only meant: "May Allah grant you success in hitting upon the truth in my affair."

And among it is the saying of Allah, exalted be His praise: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ in other verses of His revelation. It is known from this that He did not mean that He does not make clear to the wrongdoers what is obligatory upon them of His duties. And how could that be its meaning, when He has made clear to all the accountable of His creatures? Rather, He, mighty and majestic, meant that He does not grant them success, nor open their hearts to the truth and faith.

Some have claimed that the interpretation of His words ﴿Guide us﴾ is: "Increase us in guidance."

This statement cannot be free of one of two matters: either its speaker thought that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to ask his Lord for an increase in clarification, or an increase in help and success.

If he thought that he was commanded to ask his Lord for an increase in clarification, then that has no valid basis, because Allah, exalted be His praise, does not impose upon a servant any of His duties except after clarifying them to him and establishing the proof against him by it. And if its meaning were the meaning of asking for clarification, he would have been commanded to call upon his Lord to make clear to him what He had made obligatory upon him, and that is a faulty (khalaf) [[i.e., a bad form of speech. See what has passed, p. 165, no. 1.]] supplication, because He does not make an obligation except clearly stated to the one upon whom He imposes it. Or he would have been commanded to call upon his Lord to impose upon him obligations that He had not imposed.

And in the corruption of the view of the servant's request of his Lord in that, there is what makes clear that the meaning of ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ is other than the meaning of: "Make clear to us Your obligations and Your limits."

Or he thought that he was commanded to ask his Lord for an increase in help and success. If that is so, then his request for that increase cannot be free of being a request for an increase in help over what has already passed of his deeds, or over what will occur.

And in the lifting of the servant's need for help regarding what has already been concluded of his deeds [[irtafa'a al-amr: it ceased and went away, as if it had been present and then lifted. From it: the disagreement between them was lifted.]], there is what shows that the meaning of the request for that increase is only his request for an increase regarding what will occur of his deeds. Since that is so, the matter reverts to what we described and said about it: that it is the servant's request of his Lord for success in performing what he has been charged with of duties, in what lies ahead of his life.

And in the soundness of that is the corruption of the view of the people of qadar (divine decree), who claim that every one commanded with a command or charged with an obligation has already been given help in it, such that in that obligation his need for his Lord is lifted. For if the matter were as they said, the meaning of Allah's words, exalted be His praise, ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. Guide us to the straight path﴾ would be void. And in the soundness of the meaning of that, according to what we have shown, is the corruption of their statement.

Some have claimed that the meaning of His words ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ is: "Lead us on the road to Paradise in the return; that is, bring it near to us and proceed with us toward it," just as He, exalted be His praise, said: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [Surah al-Saffat: 23], meaning: "Lead them into the Fire," as a woman is led (tuhda) to her husband, meaning she is brought in to him, and as a gift is brought (tuhda) to a man, and as the leg is guided by the foot. It is like the saying of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd:

"The torrents have played over it after me,
and there ran in its radiance its rain-showers." [[From the Diwan of the Six Pre-Islamic Poets, pp. 234, 237; the first line is the opening of the poem, the last its closing. The pronoun in "laʿibat" refers to the campsite in verses that preceded. Ronaq of a sword, youth or plants: its clarity, beauty and water. It is also narrated as "fi rayq". Rayq al-shabab: its beginning, its glitter and freshness. He means luxuriant vegetation, as if he says: "in one of freshness." Al-rahm (with kasra on the ra') is the plural of rahma: a weak, continuous light rain, which is nourishing to plants. He says: the land became green with pasture, and the rain water ran through the growth, shimmering. The pronoun in "rahmuhu" refers to the rain, absent yet as if mentioned.]]
For the youth there is an intellect by which he lives,
wherever his foot guides his leg." [[He says: wherever the youth travels, he lives by his intellect, planning and striving.]]

That is: wherever it brings it to its watering places.

And in the words of Allah, exalted be His praise, ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ there is what indicates the error of this interpretation, along with the testimony of the proof from the exegetes in refuting it. For all the exegetes from the Companions and the Successors agree that the meaning of "the path" in this place is other than the meaning that the speaker of this statement interpreted, and that His words "You alone we ask for help" are the servant's request of his Lord for help in his worship. Likewise His words "Guide us" are only a request for steadfastness upon guidance in what remains of his life.

The Arabs say: "I guided so-and-so the road," "I guided him to the road," and "I guided him to the road," when you direct him to it and make the way straight for him. And the Qur'an came with all of these. Allah, exalted be His praise, said: ﴿And they say: "Praise be to Allah, who guided us to this"﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 43], and He said in another place: ﴿He chose him and guided him to a straight path﴾ [Surah al-Nahl: 121], and He said: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾.

All of that is widespread in their speech and found in their language. Among it is the saying of the poet:

"I seek forgiveness from Allah for a sin I cannot count,
Lord of the servants, to Him is the face and the deed." [[It comes in the interpretation of the verse of Surah Al 'Imran: 121, and the verse of Surah al-Qasas: 88. Sibawayh 1:17; al-Khizana 1:486. It is one of the fifty verses of Sibawayh whose speaker is unknown. Al-Shantamari said: "He meant 'for a sin', so he dropped the preposition and let the verb reach the object in the accusative." The sin here is a collective noun meaning the plural, which is why he said "I cannot count it." "Wajh" here: intention and aim, and it means turning toward.]]

He means: "I seek forgiveness of Allah for a sin," just as He, exalted be His praise, said: ﴿And seek forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Surah Ghafir: 55].

Among it is the saying of al-Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan:

"So he hunts for us the wild ass made proud by its swiftness,
before exhaustion, and the goat with its horns split." [[The verse is not in his Diwan. Among the verses of the poem there are verses in it (23), (Muhammad Jamal edition), and al-Mujtana by Ibn Durayd: 23, describing a horse. The wild ass: the onager. Al-hadr: intense running; the onager is very swift in running. Al-wani: weariness and lassitude in running or work. Al-ash'ab: a gazelle whose horns have separated and split apart in great distance. The gazelle "nabaha" when it cries out repeatedly from exuberance and vigour. When a gazelle grows old and its horns develop branches, it is called "nabih" (al-Hayawan 1:349). He describes his horse's fierce speed, overtaking the proud wild ass with its swiftness, and the firmly established swift gazelle, so that he hunts it before weariness reaches him.]]

He means: "so he hunts for us." And that is common in their poetry and speech, and in what we have mentioned of it there is sufficiency.

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿the straight path﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: The whole community of the people of interpretation has agreed that "the straight path" is the clear road that has no crookedness in it. And likewise it is in the language of all the Arabs. Among that is the saying of Jarir ibn 'Atiyya al-Khatafi:

"The commander of the believers is upon a path,
when the watering routes are crooked, it is straight." [[From his Diwan, p. 507, praising Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik. The mawarid (watering routes) are the plural of mawrida: the roads to water. He means the roads people take to their aims and needs, as they take the watering routes to water.]]

He means: "upon the road of truth." And among it is the saying of the Hudhali, Abu Dhu'ayb:

"We dawned upon their land with horses, until
we left it narrower than the path." [[It is not in his Diwan. Al-Qurtubi in his tafsir 1:128 attributes it to 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, and it is not in his Diwan. If it is Hudhali, then perhaps it is from the poetry of al-Mutanakhkhil, who has a qasida in Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 2:18-28 with this rhyme. 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib has similar verses which al-Qali narrated in al-Nawadir 3:191.]]

And among it is the saying of the reciter (rajiz):

"So turn away from the way of the straight, direct path." [[Al-Qurtubi narrated it in his tafsir 1:128, "al-sirat al-wadih" (the clear path).]]

The evidences for that are more than can be counted, and in what we have mentioned there is sufficiency from what we have left out.

Then the Arabs use "the path" figuratively, applying it to every speech and deed described as straight or crooked, so they describe the straight by its straightness and the crooked by its crookedness.

And the interpretation of this verse that is most preferable to me, namely ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, is that it means: "Grant us success in steadfastness upon what You have approved and what You granted success to those upon whom You bestowed favour among Your servants, of speech and deed, and that is the straight path." For whoever is granted success in what Allah granted success to those He favoured among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, has been granted success in Islam, in affirming the messengers, in holding fast to the Book, in acting upon what Allah commanded, in refraining from what He forbade, in following the method of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the path of Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, and every righteous servant of Allah. All of that is from the straight path.

The interpreters of the Qur'an have differed about the one meant by "the straight path" [[tarajima al-Qur'an: plural of tarjuman, and he means the exegetes; see what passed: 70, note 1]]. What we have chosen of interpretation in it includes the meanings of all of them.

Among what has been said about that is what was related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said, and mentioned the Qur'an, and said: it is the straight path.

174 - Musa ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Masruqi related this to us, saying: Husayn al-Ju'fi related to us, from Hamza al-Zayyat, from Abu al-Mukhtar al-Ta'i, from the nephew of al-Harith, from al-Harith, from 'Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ). [[Hadith 174: its isnad is very weak. Musa ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Masruqi: trustworthy; al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Khuzayma and others related from him. He died in 258 AH, biographed in al-Tahdhib. Husayn al-Ju'fi: Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn al-Walid, a well-known trustworthy narrator; Ahmad, Ibn Ma'in and others related from him, and Ibn 'Uyayna related from him although he was older than him. The compilers of the six books narrated from him. Hamza al-Zayyat: Hamza ibn Habib, the well-known reciter. Some have spoken about the narration of some of them, but the truth is that he is trustworthy, and Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih. Abu al-Mukhtar al-Ta'i: it is said his name is Sa'd; he is unknown, and al-Madini and Abu Zur'a deemed him unknown. The nephew of al-Harith al-A'war: even more unknown than that; neither he nor his father is named. His uncle al-Harith: Ibn 'Abdullah al-A'war al-Hamdani, and he is very weak. The scholars differed greatly about him, to the extent that al-Sha'bi and others described him as "a liar." I have shown in the explanation of hadith 565 and elsewhere in the Musnad that he is very weak.

As for the text of the hadith: it was related in meaning by Ibn Abi Hatim, from al-Hasan ibn 'Arafa, from Yahya ibn Yaman, from Hamza al-Zayyat, with this isnad, as reported by Ibn Kathir 1:50, where the isnad there is garbled. It is part of a long hadith on the virtues of the Qur'an, which al-Tirmidhi related (4:51-52 of Tuhfat al-Ahwadhi), from 'Abd ibn Humayd, from Husayn al-Ju'fi, with this isnad. al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a strange hadith; we do not know it except from the hadith of Hamza al-Zayyat, and its isnad is unknown, and there is discussion about the hadith of al-Harith." Likewise al-Darimi related it in his Sunan 2:435, from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Rifa'i, from Husayn al-Ju'fi. Al-Suyuti mentioned it (1:15) and attributed it also to Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman. al-Dhahabi also pointed to it in al-Mizan 3:380 in the biography of Abu al-Mukhtar al-Ta'i, saying: "His hadith on the virtues of the Qur'an is munkar." Ibn Kathir mentioned it in al-Fada'il (14-15), citing al-Tirmidhi and his weakening of it, then said: "Hamza ibn Habib al-Zayyat was not alone in narrating it; Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated it from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi from al-Harith al-A'war. Thus Hamza is free of its burden, though he is weak in hadith, he is an imam in recitation. The hadith is famous through the narration of al-Harith al-A'war, and they have spoken about him, indeed some have called him a liar regarding his opinion and creed, but as for deliberately lying in hadith, no. The most that this hadith can be is a saying of the Commander of the Believers 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and some erred in raising it, and it is a good, sound statement."

And there will come 175 and 176 with two other isnads, stopped at 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) as his own words.

The narration of Ibn Ishaq that Ibn Kathir pointed to is the hadith in Ahmad's Musnad, no. 565, from Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim ibn Sa'd, from his father, from Ibn Ishaq. We weakened its isnad there, by al-Harith al-A'war, and by its disconnection between Ibn Ishaq and Muhammad ibn Ka'b. And it does not contain the wording found here, regarding the interpretation of "the straight path."]]

175 - It was related to me from Isma'il ibn Abi Karima, who said: Muhammad ibn Salama related to us, from Abu Sinan, from 'Amr ibn Murra, from Abu al-Bakhtari, from al-Harith, from 'Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it. [[Hadith 175: It is the previous hadith with another isnad. This isnad is good up to al-Harith al-A'war, but the hadith is then made very weak by him, as we said before.

Muhammad ibn Salama: al-Bahili al-Harrani, trustworthy; Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others related from him, and Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih; he died in 191. His teacher Abu Sinan: Sa'id ibn Sinan al-Shaybani, trustworthy; whoever spoke against him did so only because of some slight error on his part. Abu Dawud said: "trustworthy, among the excellent people," and Muslim narrated from him in the Sahih. 'Amr ibn Murra: al-Muradi al-Jamali, unquestionably trustworthy and reliable; Mis'ar said: "'Amr is among the mines of truthfulness." Abu al-Bakhtari, with a fatha on the ba' and a ta' between them with a silent dotted kha': Sa'id ibn Fayruz al-Ta'i al-Kufi, a well-known trustworthy Successor.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 6 (part 2 of 2):

176 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, saying: Hamzah al-Zayyat related to us, from Abu al-Mukhtar al-Ta'i, from the nephew of al-Harith al-A'war, from al-Harith, from Ali, who said: "The straight path: the Book of God, may His remembrance be exalted." [[The report 176 is the hadith preceding it with the two chains before it, in its meaning. But here it is mawquf (halted) upon Ibn Abi Talib. The chain to him is broken in the same way as the chain of 174, because of al-Harith al-A'war and his nephew. As for those below them, Abu al-Mukhtar al-Ta'i and Hamzah continue as in 174, and Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri and Ahmad ibn Ishaq continue as in 159.]]

177 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us -[ḥ]- and Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Abu Wa'il, who said: Abd Allah said: "The straight path" is the Book of God. [[The report 177 is mawquf, a statement of Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. al-Tabari transmitted it by two chains to Sufyan, who is al-Thawri. As for the first: Ahmad ibn Ishaq from Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri from Sufyan al-Thawri, its chain is sound, with no objection to it. As for the second: Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi from Mihran, who is Ibn Abi Umar al-Attar, we have explained in chain 11 that there is confusion (idtirab) in Mihran's transmission from al-Thawri, but here he was followed in his narration by a reliable memorizer, Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri. Al-Thawri also transmitted it from Mansur, who is Ibn al-Mu'tamir al-Kufi, a reliable, firm and authoritative narrator about whom no one disagrees. Abu Wa'il is Shaqiq ibn Salamah al-Asadi, one of the senior reliable Successors. Ibn Ma'in said: "Reliable; one is not questioned about someone like him."
This report was transmitted by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:258 by way of Umar ibn Sa'd Abu Dawud al-Hadrami from al-Thawri, with this chain. He said: "This is a sahih hadith according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi agreed. al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1:15, and al-Shawkani, 1:13.]]

178 - Mahmud ibn Khidash al-Talaqani related to me, saying: Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Ru'asi related to us, saying: Ali and al-Hasan, the two sons of Salih, both related to us, from Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Aqil, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah: "Guide us to the straight path" [﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾], he said: Islam; he said: it is wider than what is between the heaven and the earth. [[The report 178 is mawquf upon Jabir ibn Abd Allah, and its chain is sound: Mahmud ibn Khidash (with a kasra on the unmarked kha and fatha on the dal, ending in shin) al-Talaqani is reliable, of the people of truthfulness; he died on Wednesday, 14 Sha'ban 250, as in al-Tarikh al-Saghir of al-Bukhari, p. 247. Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Ru'asi is reliable, firm and sensible; Ahmad and other memorizers related from him. al-Hasan and Ali, the sons of Salih ibn Salih ibn Hayy, are both reliable, and they are twin brothers. Whoever criticized al-Hasan spoke without evidence; we have declared him reliable in al-Musnad (2403), and his brother in it (220). Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Aqil ibn Abi Talib, whose mother was Zaynab al-Sughra bint Ali ibn Abi Talib, is a reliable Successor, and there is no proof for those who criticized him.
The report was transmitted by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:258-259, by way of Abu Nu'aym from al-Hasan ibn Salih alone, with this chain. He said: "This is a hadith whose chain is sahih, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi agreed. Ibn Kathir mentioned it, 1:50, and al-Suyuti, 1:15, and al-Shawkani, 1:13.]]

179 - Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Uthman ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Bishr ibn Umarah related to us, saying: Abu Rawq related to us, from al-Dahhak, from Abd Allah ibn Abbas, who said: Gabriel said to Muhammad: Say, O Muhammad: "Guide us to the straight path" [﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾], meaning: Inspire us to the guiding way, which is the religion of God, which has no crookedness. [[The hadith 179: its chain is weak, and its weakness was explained earlier (137). Ibn Kathir, 1:50, transmitted this wording without chain or attribution. al-Suyuti, 1:14, transmitted it abridged and attributed it only to al-Tabari.]]

180 - Musa ibn Sahl al-Razi related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Awf related to us, from al-Furat ibn al-Sa'ib, from Maymun ibn Mihran, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: "Guide us to the straight path" [﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾], he said: That is Islam. [[The report 180: its chain is very weak, along with our ignorance of the status of some of its narrators. Musa ibn Sahl al-Razi, the shaykh of al-Tabari: we have not determined which man he is. Perhaps he is "Musa ibn Sahl ibn Qadim, also called Ibn Musa Abu Umar al-Ramli, originally from Nasa," who is a shaykh of al-Tabari listed in al-Tahdhib 10:347, but he is not described as "al-Razi." In the manuscript it is written "Sahl ibn Musa"! We have not found this biography either, and we think it is a scribal error. Yahya ibn Awf: we have found no biography under this name at all in our available sources. As for the defect of the chain, it is al-Furat ibn al-Sa'ib al-Jazari, who is very weak. al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir 4/1/130: "They abandoned him; munkar al-hadith." The imams said the same about him. Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (folio 187): he used to narrate fabrications from the reliable and bring mu'dal reports from the trustworthy; it is not permissible to argue with him, nor to narrate from him, nor to write his hadith except as a test. As for Maymun ibn Mihran, he is a well-known reliable Successor, a jurist and proof.
This report was transmitted by Ibn Kathir, 1:50, with an unidentified wording: "It was said: it is Islam." al-Suyuti, 1:15, attributed it to Ibn Jurayj alone, with a printing error in it: "Ibn Jurayj"!]]

181 - Mahmud ibn Khidash related to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Rabi'ah al-Kilabi related to us, from Isma'il al-Azraq, from Abu Umar al-Bazzar, from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, concerning His saying: "Guide us to the straight path" [﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾], he said: It is the religion of God, which accepts from the servants nothing other than it. [[Ibn al-Hanafiyyah is Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib; al-Hanafiyyah is his mother, Khawlah bint Ja'far of the Banu Hanifah, and he became known by her name. This chain to him is weak: Muhammad ibn Rabi'ah al-Kilabi al-Ru'asi is reliable, one of the shaykhs of Ahmad and Ibn Ma'in. Isma'il al-Azraq is Isma'il ibn Salman, and he is weak; Ibn Ma'in said: "His hadith is nothing," and Ibn Numayr and al-Nasa'i said: "abandoned (matruk)." Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (p. 78, no. 35): "He is alone in strange reports he narrates from well-known figures." Abu Umar al-Bazzar is Dinar ibn Umar al-Asadi al-Kufi, the blind, and he is reliable. Ibn Kathir, 1:51, mentioned the report without attribution or chain.]]

182 - Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani related to me, saying: Amr ibn Talhah al-Qannad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi -in a report he mentioned- from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas -and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud -and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "Guide us to the straight path" [﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾], he said: It is Islam. [[The report 182 is from the tafsir of al-Suddi, and its chain was explained earlier (168). Ibn Kathir, 1:50, and al-Suyuti, 1:15, transmitted it.]]
