183 - al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan related to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Dawud related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraj, who said: Ibn Abbas said concerning His saying: "Guide us to the straight path" [﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾], he said: The way. [[The report 183 was transmitted by al-Suyuti, 1:14, attributed to al-Tabari and Ibn al-Mundhir. The beginning of this chain was mentioned earlier (144). It is here disconnected (munqati'), because Ibn Juraj did not meet Ibn Abbas; he only narrates from those who narrated from him.]]

184 - Abd Allah ibn Kathir Abu Sudayf al-Amuli related to us, saying: Hashim ibn al-Qasim related to us, saying: Hamzah ibn al-Mughirah related to us, from Asim, from Abu al-Aliyah, concerning His saying: "Guide us to the straight path" [﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾], he said: It is the Messenger of God ﷺ, and his two companions after him, Abu Bakr and Umar. He said: I mentioned that to al-Hasan, and he said: Abu al-Aliyah spoke truly and sincerely. [[The report 184: Abd Allah ibn Kathir Abu Sudayf al-Amuli, a shaykh of al-Tabari: I did not know who he is, and found no mention of him; I fear there may be a distortion in it. Hashim ibn al-Qasim is Abu al-Nadr (with an n and a emphatic-less sad, i.e., with the letter sad marked), the memorizer, the Khurasani imam, shaykh of the imams Ahmad, Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn al-Madini, Ibn Ma'in and others.
Hamzah ibn al-Mughirah ibn Nushayt (with fatha on the nun and kasra on the marked shin), the Kufan worshipper: reliable, biographied in al-Tahdhib; al-Bukhari biographied him in al-Kabir 2/1/44, Ibn Abi Hatim in 1/2/214-215, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat 443, saying: "Hamzah ibn al-Mughirah the worshipper, from the people of Kufa. He narrates from Asim al-Ahwal from Abu al-Aliyah ('guide us to the straight path'), he said: it is the Prophet ﷺ and his two companions. Abu al-Nadr Hashim ibn al-Qasim narrated from him." In the originals it occurs here as "Hamzah ibn Abi al-Mughirah," which is an error of the copyists.
Asim is Ibn Sulayman al-Ahwal, a reliable, firm Successor. Abu al-Aliyah is al-Riyahi (with a kasra on the ra and lightened ya), named Rufay' (diminutive) ibn Mihran, one of the senior reliable Successors, whose reliability is agreed upon.
This report was mentioned by Ibn Kathir, 1:51, who also attributed it to Ibn Abi Hatim; and al-Suyuti, 1:15, who added its attribution to Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Adi and Ibn Asakir. Abu al-Aliyah did not say it on his own: al-Hakim transmitted it in al-Mustadrak 2:259 by way of Abu al-Nadr with this chain to "Abu al-Aliyah from Ibn Abbas." He said: "This is a hadith whose chain is sahih, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi agreed. al-Suyuti abridged it and attributed it only to al-Hakim.]]

185 - Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Guide us to the straight path" [﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾], he said: Islam. [[The report 185 is a statement of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ibn Kathir, 1:51, transmitted it without attribution. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd is late, one of the followers of the Successors, died in 182 AH. He is very weak; I explained his weakness in the hadith of al-Musnad (5723), and it suffices from him the saying of Ibn Khuzaymah: "He is not someone whose hadith the people of knowledge argue with, due to his poor memory; he is a man whose occupation is worship and asceticism, not one of the intimates of hadith."]]

186 - al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to me, that Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr narrated to him, from his father, from Nawwas ibn Sam'an al-Ansari, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: God struck a parable: a straight path. And the path: is Islam.

187 - al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Adam al-Asqalani related to us, saying: al-Layth related to us, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from his father, from Nawwas ibn Sam'an al-Ansari, from the Prophet ﷺ, similarly. [[Hadiths 186 and 187: al-Tabari transmitted them from his shaykh "al-Muthanna" by two chains, the first higher in rank than the second: between al-Muthanna and Mu'awiyah ibn Salih there is one shaykh in the first, and two shaykhs in the second.
As for al-Muthanna, the shaykh of al-Tabari: he is al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim al-Amuli, from whom al-Tabari narrates much in tafsir and history. Abu Salih in the first chain is Abd Allah ibn Salih al-Misri, scribe of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, who accompanied him for twenty years. He is reliable; whoever criticized him, for some of his narrations from al-Layth, spoke without evidence. He has a good biography in al-Tahdhib, and likewise in Ibn Abi Hatim's al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 2/2/86-87, and Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1:351-353. Abd Allah ibn Salih was born in 137 and died in 222. The date of his birth occurs in al-Tahdhib (173), which is a printing error; the correct one is in Tadhkirat al-Huffaz. Adam al-Asqalani in the second chain is Adam ibn Abi Iyas, who is reliable, trustworthy and devout, one of the best servants of God, as Abu Hatim said. al-Layth is Ibn Sa'd, imam of the people of Egypt. Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, in both chains, is al-Himsi, one of the great scholars and judge of al-Andalus, reliable; whoever criticized him was mistaken. Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr (diminutive in both) al-Hadrami al-Himsi is a reliable Successor. His father is one of the senior Successors, who lived in the time of the Prophet ﷺ; he is reliable and well known for knowledge, and al-Tabari mentioned him in Tabaqat al-Fuqaha. Nawwas (with a fatha on the nun and shadda on the waw) ibn Sam'an al-Kilabi is a well-known Companion.
This hadith is an abridgement of a long hadith, transmitted by Ahmad in al-Musnad 17711 (vol. 4, p. 182, Halabi edition) from al-Hasan ibn Sawwar from al-Layth ibn Sa'd from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, with it. Ibn Kathir, 1:51, transmitted it from the Musnad version, saying: "Thus did Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir narrate it from the hadith of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, with it. And al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i both narrated it from Ali ibn Hujr ibn Baqiyyah from Bujayr ibn Sa'd from Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Jubayr ibn Nufayr from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, with it. It is a sound, sahih chain." al-Suyuti, 1:15, and al-Shawkani, 1:13, also attributed it to al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and to others.]]

Abu Ja'far said: God only described it as "straight" because it is correct, with no error in it. Some foolish people have claimed that He named it "straight" because it leads its people straight to Paradise. But that is an interpretation which opposes the interpretation of all the people of tafsir, and their unanimous agreement against it is sufficient proof of its error.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 7 (part 1 of 4):

The explanation of His saying: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾.

His saying ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is a clarification of "the straight path": which path is it, since every road of truth is a straight path? It was said to Muhammad ﷺ: "Say, O Muhammad: Guide us, O our Lord, to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, by Your obedience and worship, from among Your angels, Your prophets, the truthful (al-siddiqin), the martyrs and the righteous."

This is similar to what our Lord, may His praise be exalted, said in His revelation: ﴿And if they had done what they were admonished with, it would have been better for them and stronger in firming (their faith). And then We would have given them from Us a great reward. And We would have guided them to a straight path. And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those will be with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous.﴾ [Surah al-Nisa' 4:66–69].

Abu Ja'far said: The guidance to the straight path which Muhammad ﷺ and his community were commanded to ask their Lord for is the guidance to the path whose description Allah, may His praise be exalted, gave. That path is the path of those whom Allah described with what He described them in His revelation, and whom He promised, if they travelled it and remained steadfast in it, obeying Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, that He would bring to their destinations; and Allah does not break His promise.

Reports in agreement with what we have said on this have been related from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

188 – Muhammad ibn al-'Ala' narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to us, saying: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: "The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" – he said: the way of those upon whom You bestowed favour by Your obedience and worship, from among the angels, the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, who obeyed You and worshipped You.[[The report 188: The weakness of this chain is detailed in no. 137. This report was also transmitted by Ibn Kathir 1:52. See also no. 179.]]

189 – Ahmad ibn Hazim al-Ghifari narrated to me, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa informed us, from Abu Ja'far, from Rabi': "The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" – he said: the prophets.[[The report 189: Rabi' is Ibn Anas al-Bakri; his chain was explained earlier at no. 164. This report was transmitted by Ibn Kathir 1:53 and al-Suyuti 1:16.]]

190 – al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "upon whom You have bestowed favour" – he said: the believers.[[The report 190: Like report 183, this is a broken chain between Ibn Jurayj and Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Kathir 1:53 and al-Suyuti 1:16 also transmitted it, but in their texts "Ibn Humayd" appears in place of "Ibn Jarir".]]

191 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Waki' said: "upon whom You have bestowed favour" – the Muslims.[[The report 191: Ibn Kathir also transmitted this report, 1:53.]]

192 – Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said, concerning Allah's saying "The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour": the Prophet ﷺ and those with him.[[The report 192: This chain has passed at no. 185. The text of the report is in Ibn Kathir 1:53, who said after these reports: "The explanation earlier from Ibn 'Abbas is more general and comprehensive," meaning report 188.]]

Abu Ja'far said: This verse is clear evidence that the obedience of Allah, may His praise be exalted, is not attained by those who obey except by Allah's bestowing it upon them and His granting them success in it. Do they not hear Him say "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour", attributing to His favour every guidance, obedience and worship that came from them?

If someone says: Where is the complement of this statement? You know that when one says to another "I have favoured you", it requires mention of what he was favoured with. So where is that mention in "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour"? And what is the favour which He bestowed upon them?

It is said to him: We have already set out earlier in this book the Arabs' practice in their speech of letting one part stand for another when the apparent part indicates the hidden part and suffices for it. His saying "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" is of this kind. Because Allah's command to His servants to ask Him for help, and their request of Him for guidance to the straight path, preceded His saying "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" – which is a clarification of the straight path and a substitution for it – it is known that the favour which Allah bestowed upon those whose path we were commanded to ask to be guided to is the clear course and the straight path whose interpretation we have set out just above. So what manifestly appears of that, together with the closeness of the two phrases, suffices without repeating it.

As the Nabigha of the Banu Dhubyan said:

"As if you were, of the camels of Banu Uqaysh, / a camel whose hind legs are rattled with a waterskin."[[Diwan: 58; Sibawayh 1:375; Majaz al-Qur'an: 101; al-Khizana 2:314. The poet said this to 'Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari. Banu Uqaysh: they are the Banu Uqaysh ibn 'Ubayd; it was also said they are a clan of Ash'ar, and it was said they are a tribe of Yemen whose camels are very skittish; and it was said they are a tribe of jinn, as they claim. "Qa'qa'a" means to shake something dry so that a sound is heard from it. "Shann" means an old, worn waterskin. He describes 'Uyayna as cowardly, weak and in extreme terror, like a very skittish camel when it hears the sound of a waterskin being rattled.]]

He means: "As if you were, of the camels of Banu Uqaysh, a camel whose hind legs are rattled with a waterskin." He suffices with the apparent mention of "camels", which indicates the omitted element, from showing what was omitted. And as al-Farazdaq ibn Ghalib said:

"You see their cords, worn across their shoulders, / when the iron of the warriors rusts."[[Diwan: 131; al-Naqa'id: 773. It occurs in the interpretation of a verse of Surat al-Shu'ara' 4 (19:38 Bulaq), where it reads "on the book," which is an error. He satirises Jarir and his people, Banu Kulayb ibn Yarbu'. "Arbaq" is the plural of "rabq," and "rabq" is the plural of "ribqa": a rope with which young sheep are tied so they do not suckle. "Taqallada al-sayf" means he placed its sword-hilt on his shoulder. "Kumat" is the plural of "kamı": a champion of great fierceness. He describes Banu Kulayb as lowly, miserly shepherds, whose only concern is tending sheep, while the heroes in war endure its heat for long days until the iron of the armour rusts on their bodies from sweat.]]

He means: "their cords, they are wearing them", so he omitted "they", since the apparent "their cords" indicates it.

The evidence for this from the poetry and speech of the Arabs is more than can be counted. Likewise is this in His saying "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour."

* *

The explanation of His saying: ﴿not of those who have evoked anger﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: The readers agree on reading "ghayr" with a kasra on its final letter [[In the printed edition: "والقراء مجمعة", and "al-qaraʾa" is the plural of "qari'". See above p. 51 note, and p. 64 note 4 and p. 109 note 1.]]. The genitive case of it comes from two directions:

The first: that "ghayr" be an attribute (sifa) of "alladhina" and a qualifier (na't) of them, so you put it in the genitive, since "alladhina" is in the genitive and it is a qualifier and description of them. It is permissible for "ghayr" to qualify "alladhina" even though "alladhina" is definite and "ghayr" is indefinite, because "alladhina" with its relative clause is not a specific definite like proper names that are signs among people, such as Zayd and 'Amr and the like [[He means by "specific definite" the determinate definite, which is the proper name that identifies its referent absolutely and without restriction. So your saying "Zayd" identifies absolutely or determinately. What is defined with the article "al-" identifies its referent only so long as "al-" is in it; when it is detached, the identification goes. See al-Farra's Ma'ani 1:7.]]; rather, it is like indefinite unknown nouns, such as "al-rajul" and "al-ba'ir" and the like. Since "alladhina" is like that in its description, and "ghayr" is attached to an unknown noun, analogous to "alladhina" in being an indefinite, non-specific definite, just as "alladhina" is an indefinite, non-specific definite, it is permissible on that account that "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim" be a qualifier of "alladhina an'amta 'alayhim", as one says: "I do not sit except with the scholar who is not ignorant," meaning: I sit only with one who knows, not with one who is ignorant.

If "alladhina an'amta 'alayhim" were a specific definite, it would not be permissible for "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim" to be a qualifier of it. That is because it is an error in Arabic speech, when you describe a specific definite with an indefinite, to make its qualifier, the indefinite, take the case of the definite it qualifies, unless one intends to repeat the governing element of the qualified noun. It would be an error in their speech to say "I passed by 'Abd Allah ghayr al-'alim", putting "ghayr" in the genitive, except with the intention of repeating the preposition "bi" which governed "'Abd Allah". So the meaning, were it said that way, would be: "I passed by 'Abd Allah, I passed by one who is not learned." This is the first of the two genitive readings of "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim".

The second of the two genitive readings is that "alladhina" be taken in the sense of a specific definite. When it is directed to that, "ghayr" is in the genitive by intending to repeat "al-sirat", the word which "alladhina" was put in the genitive after. It is as if you said: "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, the path of those not evoking anger."

These two interpretations of "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim", although they differ in accordance with the difference in their grammatical analysis, their meanings are close. This is because whoever Allah has favoured and guided to His true religion has been safe from the anger of his Lord and has been saved from error in his religion.

So it is equal – since the reason for his saying "Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" makes it impossible for the hearer, while hearing it from the reciter, to doubt that those whom Allah has favoured with guidance to the path are not people whose Lord is angry with them, together with the favour whose magnitude He has made great upon them in their religion; nor that they are astray while their Lord has guided them to the truth – since it is impossible in their natural constitution for pleasure from Allah, may His praise be exalted, toward a person and anger toward him to coexist at one time, or for guidance and error to coexist in him at one time – whether the people are described [[The phrase reads: "it is equal... whether the people are described... or not described", and between these two is a long digression, as is Abu Ja'far's habit in his exposition.]] together with His description of them with what He described them with of His granting them success and His guidance to them, and His favour upon them with what Allah bestowed upon them in their religion, as being "not those who have evoked anger, nor those who are astray"; or whether they are not described by that. Because the apparent attribute by which they were described has informed about them that they are so, even if the description does not state it explicitly.

This applies when we direct "ghayr" to the reading in which it is in the genitive by intending to repeat "al-sirat" which governs "alladhina", and we do not make "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa la al-dallin" an attribute of "alladhina an'amta 'alayhim", but rather when we take them as other than those, even though both groups are undoubtedly favoured in their religions.

As for when we direct "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa la al-dallin" to being a qualifier of "alladhina an'amta 'alayhim", then the hearer has no need for inference, since the explicit sense of its meaning has already sufficed as evidence.

It is also permissible to read "ghayr" in "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim" in the accusative, although I dislike reciting with it because it deviates from the readings of the readers. Whatever readings deviate from what the community has transmitted by clear and widely attested transmission is an opinion opposed to the truth, and a departure from the way of Allah, the way of His Messenger ﷺ and the way of the Muslims. Yet if it were permissible to recite with it [[In the printed edition: "if the recitation were permissible with it", altered to match their wording rather than al-Tabari's]], there would still be a sound way to justify it.

The interpretation of its correct form when you read it in the accusative: it is directed to being an attribute of the hā' and mīm in "'alayhim", which refer to "alladhina". For although it is in the genitive by "'ala", it is in a position of accusative by the verb "an'amta". So the sense of the statement, when you read "ghayr" which is with "al-maghdubi 'alayhim" in the accusative, is: "the path of those whom You guided, a favour from You upon them, not evoking anger upon them", that is, neither evoking anger upon them nor being astray. The accusative in that case is then like the accusative in "ghayr" in your saying: "I passed by 'Abd Allah, not the noble nor the upright", where you separate "ghayr al-karim" from "'Abd Allah", since "'Abd Allah" is a specific definite and "ghayr al-karim" is an indefinite unknown.

Some of the grammarians of Basra used to claim that the reading of whoever put "ghayr" in the accusative in "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim" was on the basis of exception from the meanings of the attribute of "alladhina an'amta 'alayhim", as if he held that the meaning intended by those who read it in the accusative was: "Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, except those evoking anger upon them, those whom You have not favoured in their religions nor guided to the truth, so do not make us among them." As the Nabigha of the Banu Dhubyan said:

"I stood in it at evening, asking it, / it was unable to answer, and there was no one in the enclosure"[[Diwan: 23; it occurs in the interpretation of Surat al-Baqara 35 (1:186 Bulaq), Surat al-Nisa' 114 (5:178), Surat Yunus 98 (11:117) and Surat al-Layl 20 (30:146). One says: "I met him uṣaylālan and uṣaylānan," when one meets him in the evening. For "uṣayl" is evening, its plural is "uṣul" and "uṣlān", then they diminutivised the plural, saying "uṣaylān", then replaced the nūn with a lām. They did this out of mastery of their Arabic, and because of their frequent use of it, until few who did not know its origin and meaning remained. "'Ayya fi mantiqihi" means he was unable to speak.]]

"except the stalls, after difficulty, I explain them with effort, / and the stone-ring is like a pool in the wronged waste, the hard ground."[[Awari is the plural of "ari" (with a doubled yā'): the enclosure and stall and tethering place of a beast, from their saying: "ta'arra bi-l-makan," he stayed and was held back. "Lata" means after effort and hardship and delay. "Nu'y" is a pit around the tent, its edges raised with earth, which holds back water so it does not enter the tent. "The wronged" means land they passed through in a desert, where they dug a pool to water their camels, and which was not a place for digging since it was far from the paths of travellers; therefore he named it "wronged". "Zulm" means placing a thing in other than its place. "Jalad" is hard ground, meaning it grows nothing, so no one grazes it.]]

It is known that "awari" is in no way counted among "ahad". Likewise, in his view, "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim" was an exception from "alladhina an'amta 'alayhim", even though they were not among its meanings in religion at all.

As for the grammarians of Kufa, they rejected this interpretation and considered it weak [[In the printed edition: "wa-istakhtha'u" (considered it wrong); "istakhaffu" means considered it light, without weight.]], and claimed that if it were as the Basran claimant said, it would be an error to say "wa la al-dallin" (and not the astray).

For "la" is negation and denial, and one does not conjoin a denial except to a denial. They said: we have not found in any of the speech of the Arabs an exception which is conjoined to by a denial; rather we have found them conjoining an exception to an exception and a denial to a denial. They say in the exception: "the people stood except your brother and except your father." And in the denial: "your brother did not stand, nor your father." As for "the people stood except your father and not your brother", we have not found it in Arabic speech. They said: since that is absent from Arabic speech, and the Qur'an was revealed in the most eloquent of the Arabic tongues, we know – since His saying "wa la al-dallin" is conjoined to His saying "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim" – that "ghayr" carries the sense of denial, not the sense of exception, and that the interpretation of whoever directed it to exception is an error.

These, then, are the interpretations of "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim", according to the differing ways of parsing it.

We have raised what we have raised concerning the explanation of its grammatical forms – although our purpose in this book is to uncover the interpretation of the Qur'anic verses – because the difference in the ways of parsing it entails a difference in the ways of interpreting it. So the need compelled us to uncover its grammatical forms, so that the seeker of its interpretation might see its interpretations, according to the variety of differing views on its interpretation and recitation.

The correct view on its interpretation and recitation, in our opinion, is the first view, which is the reading ﴿ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim﴾ with the genitive on the "r" of "ghayr" – interpreting it as an attribute of "alladhina an'amta 'alayhim" and a qualifier of them, as we have already explained – if you wish; and if you wish, by interpreting it as a repetition of "sirat". All of that is correct and good.

If someone says to us: Who are these, the ones upon whom anger is evoked, whom Allah, may His praise be exalted, has commanded us to ask that He not make us among them?

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 1, verse 7 (part 2 of 4):

It has been said: They are those whom God, may His praise be exalted, described in His revelation when He said: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from God? Those whom God cursed and with whom He was angry, and of whom He made apes and swine, and who worshipped the Taghut. Those are worse in position and further astray from the right way.﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 60]. Thus He informed us, may His remembrance be exalted, of what punishment He brought down upon them (thamma [[In the printed edition it was changed to "bimanhu" ("by His favour"); thumma and thumma (with a fatha on the tha') are used to indicate a distant place, equivalent to "huna" for a near one.]]) because of their disobedience to Him. Then He taught us, by His favour upon us, the way to salvation, so that there would not befall us the like of what befell them of the mathulat [[The mathulat are the plural of mathulah (with a fatha, then a damma, then a fatha): it means punishment and chastisement.]], and out of His compassion towards us.

If it is asked: What is the proof that they are those whom God described and whose story He mentioned in His revelation in the manner you have described? It is answered:

193 - Ahmad ibn al-Walid al-Ramli narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Ja'far al-Raqqi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan ibn Uyaynah narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from al-Sha'bi, from Adi ibn Hatim, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to me: "Those who earned anger are the Jews." [[Hadith 193 - This is a sound chain, and part of this hadith will come later with this same chain (207). Its takhrij will come at 195.]]

194 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Simak ibn Harb, who said: I heard Abbad ibn Hubaysh narrate, from Adi ibn Hatim, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to me: "Indeed, those who earned anger are the Jews." [[Hadith 194 - This is also a sound chain. Abbad ibn Hubaysh, with a dammah on the h and a fatha on the b, and a shin at the end, al-Kufi: Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat, and Ibn Abi Hatim (3/1/78). Part of the hadith will also come with this chain (208).]]

195 - Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated to me, saying: Muslim ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Mus'ab narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Simak ibn Harb, from Murri ibn Qatari, from Adi ibn Hatim, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the words of God, may He be exalted and glorified, "not of those who earned anger," and he said: "They are the Jews." [[Hadith 195 - This is also a sound chain. Murri ibn Qatari al-Kufi: Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat, and al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir (4/2/57), saying: "He heard Adi ibn Hatim; Simak ibn Harb narrated from him; he is counted among the Kufans." "Murri" is with a damma on the m and a shaddah on the r with a kasrah, and "Qatari" with fatha on the q and t, and after the r a shaddah on the y. Part of it will also come with the same chain (209).

As for this hadith from Adi ibn Hatim: its origin is a lengthy account of his conversion to Islam. Ahmad related it in full in al-Musnad (4: 378-379) from Muhammad ibn Ja'far, from Shu'bah, with the earlier chain (194). al-Tirmidhi (4: 67) related it through Amr ibn Abi Qays, from Simak, from Abbad ibn Hubaysh, from Adi, and said: "This is a good, strange hadith; we only know it from the hadith of Simak ibn Harb. Shu'bah related from Simak ibn Harb, from Abbad ibn Hubaysh, from Adi ibn Hatim, from the Prophet (ﷺ) — the hadith in full." Al-Tayalisi in his Musnad (1040) related part of it from Amr ibn Thabit, "from one who heard Adi ibn Hatim." It has become clear to us from al-Tabari's narrations here that Simak ibn Harb heard it from Abbad ibn Hubaysh and from Murri ibn Qatari, both from Adi, and that Simak ibn Harb did not alone transmit it, since Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid related it from al-Sha'bi from Adi. As for al-Tirmidhi's statement that he only knew it from Simak's hadith, this does not preclude others knowing it by another route. Ibn Kathir (1: 54) mentioned it from Ahmad's narration in al-Musnad, and pointed to al-Tirmidhi's narration and to al-Tabari's narrations here, then said: "This hadith of Adi has been related through many routes, and it has many wordings, the mention of which would be lengthy." al-Hafiz mentioned it in al-Isabah, in the biography of Adi (2: 229), from the narrations of Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi. al-Suyuti mentioned from it (1: 16) the explanation of the two letters, and attributed it also to Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih. Al-Shawkani did likewise (1: 15).]]

196 - Humayd ibn Mas'adah al-Sami narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: al-Juraygiri narrated to us, from Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq: that a man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while he was besieging the Wadi al-Qura, and said: "Who are these whom you are besieging, O Messenger of God?" He said: "These are those who earned anger, the Jews." [[Hadith 196 - Humayd ibn Mas'adah al-Sami, the teacher of al-Tabari: he is "al-Sami" with an unpointed sin, as stated by al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar in al-Taqrib. It is a nisbah to "Samah ibn Lu'ayy ibn Ghalib." In the copies of al-Tabari here and in what follows (210) it appears as "al-Shami" with a dotted letter, which is a misreading. "al-Juraygiri," with a damma on the j, is Sa'id ibn Iyas al-Basri. "Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq al-Uqayli," with a damma on the ayn and fatha on the qaf, is a major, trustworthy Successor. This chain is mursal, since Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq said: "that a man." It will also come mursal at 197 and 199, but it will come connected (mawsul) at 198.]]

197 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, from Sa'id al-Juraygiri, from Urwah, from Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq: that a man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he mentioned something similar.

198 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Budayl al-Uqayli, who said: Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq informed me that he was informed by one who heard the Prophet (ﷺ) — while he was in the Wadi al-Qura, on his horse — and a man from the Banu al-Qayn asked him: "O Messenger of God, who are these?" He said: "Those who earned anger." And he pointed to the Jews. [[Hadith 198 - Budayl, with a damma on the b and fatha on the d, is Ibn Maysarah al-Uqayli, a trustworthy Successor. This narration is connected by a sound chain, because Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq explicitly stated in it that he was informed by "one who heard the Prophet (ﷺ)," and the anonymity of a Companion is not harmful, as is well known. The connection through mention of an unnamed Companion is an addition from a trustworthy narrator, so it is accepted.

Ibn Kathir (1: 54-55) mentioned this connected narration, then pointed to the three mursal narrations, then said: "In the narration of Urwah there occurred a naming: Abd Allah ibn Amr, and Allah knows best." But he did not mention who related the narration of Urwah to which he pointed. Ibn Kathir then said: "Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Ibrahim ibn Tahman, from Budayl ibn Maysarah, from Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about those who earned anger; he said: the Jews. I said: those who went astray? He said: the Christians." al-Hafiz pointed in Fath al-Bari (8: 122) to this narration of Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Dharr "with a good chain." He also mentioned that the connected narration of Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, "that one who heard the Prophet (ﷺ) informed him," was related by Ahmad. These narrations are also in al-Suyuti (1: 16) and al-Shawkani (1: 14-15). The explanation of "those who went astray" will come through these chains at 210, 211, 212, 213. The identification of Urwah in the chain at 197 will come at 211.]]

199 - al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Khalid al-Wasiti narrated to us, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned something similar.

200 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn Umarah narrated to us, saying: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas: "not of those who earned anger," meaning the Jews, upon whom God's anger fell. [[Report 200 - The report of al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, they did not takhrij it. Its remainder will come at 215.]]

201 - Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Talhah narrated to us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas — and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud — and from some people among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "not of those who earned anger," they are the Jews. [[Report 201 - Ibn Kathir (1: 55), al-Durr al-Manthur (1: 16), and al-Shawkani (1: 15). Its remainder will come at 217.]]

202 - Ibn Humayd al-Razi narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mujahid, who said: "not of those who earned anger," he said: they are the Jews.

203 - Ahmad ibn Hazim al-Ghifari narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from Rabi': "not of those who earned anger," he said: the Jews.

204 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "not of those who earned anger," he said: the Jews.

205 - Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "not of those who earned anger," the Jews.

206 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd narrated to me, from his father, who said: "those who earned anger," the Jews. [[Reports 202-206: in Ibn Kathir, al-Durr al-Manthur, and al-Shawkani, as those already passed. Their remainder will come at 214, 216, 218, 219, 220.]]

Abu Ja'far said: They differed concerning the description of God's anger, may His remembrance be exalted:

Some of them said: God's anger toward whomever He is angry with among His creatures is the descent of His punishment upon the one with whom He is angry, either in this world or in the Hereafter, as He described Himself, may His remembrance be exalted, in His Book, when He said: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them and drowned them all.﴾ [Surah al-Zukhruf: 55].

And as He said: (Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from God? Those whom God cursed and with whom He was angry, and of whom He made apes and swine) [Surah al-Ma'idah: 60].

Others said: God's anger toward those among His servants with whom He is angry is His censure of them and of their deeds, and His reproach of them by speech.

Others said: God's anger is a meaning understood, like what is known of the meanings of anger, except that — although it is so in terms of affirmation [[Affirmation: the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah concerning affirming God's attributes as He described Himself and affirming decree without interpretation, in opposition to the Qadariyyah who deny it, and to the Jahmiyyah and the Mu'attilah who deny the attributes.]] — its meaning from Him differs from the anger of human beings, which disturbs and agitates them, troubles them, and harms them.

For God, may His praise be exalted, is not subject to afflictions in His essence, but He has an attribute, just as knowledge is an attribute of His and power is an attribute of His, as is intelligible in terms of affirmation, even though those meanings differ from the meanings of the knowledge of servants, which are the perceptions of hearts and their faculties that exist with the existence of actions and cease with their non-existence. [[After this point, the copy of the Egyptian National Library no. 100 Tafsir contains the following text:
"And may God bless Muhammad the unlettered Prophet, and his family, with abundant peace.
- from the original from which it was copied -
Heard by myself, Ahmad, Muhammad, and al-Hasan, sons of Abd Allah ibn Ahmad al-Farghani, on Thursday, seven days remaining in the month of Ramadan, in the year three hundred and forty-six. Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Tusi."]]

* *

On the interpretation of His saying, may His praise be exalted: ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: Some people of Basra claimed that "la" with "al-dallin" was introduced as a completion of the speech, and its meaning is its being superfluous, and they cited as proof for their statement the verse of al-Ajjaj: "fi bi'ri la hawrin sara wa ma sha'ar" [[His Diwan: 16; Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 8; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu Ubaydah: 25; al-Khizanah 2: 95; Amali al-Shajari 2: 231; al-Addad of Ibn al-Anbari: 186. The one who said it is superfluous among the Basrans is Abu Ubaydah.]]

And he interprets it as meaning: "in a well of hawr he travelled," i.e., in a well of perdition, and that "la" means superfluous and connective. He also argues for this with the words of Abu al-Najm:

"fa ma ulumu al-bida an la tuskhara lamma ra'ayna al-shamta al-qafandara" [[Attributed by the commentator of al-Qamus from al-Saghani to Abu al-Najm, and he said its narration is: "idha ra'at dha al-shaybah al-qafandara." They vocalized "al-shamt" with a fatha on the m, meaning white hair, and it is possible that Abu al-Najm said "al-shimt" with a kasrah on the m, as an adjective, dropping the alif of "ashmat," as they did with ash'ath and sha'th, and ahdab and hadab, and at'as and ta'as, and ahwal and hawl, in adjectives of apparent defects and ornament. See al-Faʼiq of al-Zamakhshari 2: 326, where he enumerates other such words. It seems al-Saghani refused the narration "al-shamt" with two fathas, since al-qafandar is a small-headed, ugly-looking person.

The verse with the narration of al-Biri in Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu Ubaydah: 26, al-Addad of Ibn al-Anbari: 185, and al-Lisan (q-f-n-d-r), then see Amali al-Shajari 2: 231, and others.]]

He means: "fa ma ulumu al-bida an tuskhara" (I do not blame the fair ones for not mocking). And with the words of al-Ahwas:

"wa yalhaynani fi al-lahw an la uhibbahu wa lil-lahwi da'in da'imbun ghayru ghafil" [[al-Kamil 1: 49; al-Addad of Ibn al-Anbari: 186; "lahhahu yalhahu lahan": blamed him and reproached him.]]

He means: "wa yalhaynani fi al-lahw an uhibbahu" (they blame me for loving frivolity), and with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 12], meaning "that you prostrate." It has been transmitted from the author of this view that he interpreted "ghayr" which is with "al-maghdub 'alayhim" as meaning "siwa" (other than). So the meaning of the speech according to him was: "Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, who are other than the ones who earned anger and the astray." [[He is Abu Ubaydah, as we mentioned earlier in this paragraph. al-Farra' alluded to him in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (8) saying: "Some who do not know Arabic have said..." and al-Tabari likewise did this earlier in several places. See al-Lisan (gh-y-r).]]

Some of the grammarians of Kufa rejected this statement [[He means al-Farra' the Kufan, in his book Ma'ani al-Qur'an (8), or someone else from his books.]], and claimed that "ghayr" which is with "al-maghdub 'alayhim", if it meant "siwa", it would be an error to conjoin to it with "la", since "la" is only used to conjoin upon a preceding negation, just as it would be an error for a speaker to say: "I have other than your brother nor your father," because "siwa" is not among the particles of negation and denial. He says: since that was an error in the speech of the Arabs, and the Qur'an is in the most eloquent of the Arabic languages, it is known that the claim of the one who asserted that "ghayr" with "al-maghdub 'alayhim" means "siwa al-maghdub 'alayhim" is an error, since he has turned the speech back with "la." He used to claim that "ghayr" there is only meaning negation, since it is sound in the speech of the Arabs and common and apparent in their discourse to direct "ghayr" to the sense of negation, and it is used of them: "Your brother is not good nor gracious," meaning your brother is neither good nor gracious. And he rejected that "la" should come with the meaning of omission at the beginning of speech, without a preceding negation. He says: if it were permissible for it to come in the sense of omission at the beginning, before an indication of a previous negation, it would be correct for a speaker to say: "I wanted that I not honour your brother," meaning: "I wanted to honour your brother." He used to say: in the testimony of the people of knowledge of the Arabic tongue to the error of the one who says this, there is clear evidence that "la" comes at the beginning with the meaning of omission, without a preceding negation. And he used to interpret the "la" in the verse of al-Ajjaj, which we mentioned the Basran cited, by saying: it is a correct negation, and the meaning of the verse is: he travelled in a well in which he does not benefit from anything, and no trace of work becomes clear to him in it, while he does not perceive or know of it. [[Al-Farra's words in Ma'ani al-Qur'an: "As if you said: he headed toward no right direction and did not know."]] From their saying: "The grinding millstone ground and did not produce anything," i.e., no trace of work became clear for it. He says regarding the other verses, meaning like the verse of Abu al-Najm:

"fa ma ulumu al-bida an la tuskhara"

It is only permissible for "la" to mean omission because a negation preceded it at the beginning of the speech, so the latter speech was joined to the former, as the poet said:

"ma kana yarda Rasul Allah fi'lahum wa al-tayyibani Abu Bakr wa la Umar"

[[The verse is by Jarir satirizing al-Akhtal; his Diwan 263; Naqa'id Jarir wa al-Akhtal: 174; al-Addad of Ibn al-Anbari: 186; then the tafsir of the verse of Surah al-Baqarah: 158.]]

Thus it was permissible, since the negation had preceded at the beginning of the speech.

Abu Ja'far said: This latter view is closer to the truth than the first, since in the speech of the Arabs it is not established that a sentence begins without a negation preceding it with "lā" (which carries the meaning of negation), nor is it permissible to conjoin it by "lā" to "siwā" (other than), or to the particle of exception. In the speech of the Arabs, "ghayr" has three meanings: first, exception; second, negation; and third, "siwā" (other than). Since it is established that the error of "lā" is that it cannot be used with the meaning of nullification (ilghā') as a beginning, and since it is incorrect for it to be a conjunction to "ghayr" which is with "al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim", if it were in the sense of "illā" which is an exception; and it is also not permissible for it to be a conjunction to it if it were in the sense of "siwā", while "lā" would exist as a conjunction by the "wāw" which conjoins it to what precedes it—[this is the answer to his saying "if the error is established..."] it is correct, and it is established that there is no way for "ghayr", which is with "al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim", to be directed toward it in a manner that is valid with "illā" in the sense of negation and denial, and that there is no way for His saying "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn" except as a conjunction to "ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim."

So the interpretation of the speech, since what we have said is correct by what we have cited as evidence, is: "Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray."

If someone says to us: Who are these astray (al-ḍāllūn) whom God has commanded us to seek refuge in God from, that He should lead us upon their way, or that we should go astray in their straying?

It is said: They are those whom God described in His revelation, saying: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, do not exceed the bounds in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray, and strayed from the right way﴾ [Surah al-Mā'idah: 77].

If he says: What is your proof that they are these?

It is said:

207 – Aḥmad ibn al-Walīd al-Ramlī narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah narrated to us, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, from al-Shaʿbī, from ʿAdī ibn Abī Ḥātim, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn" – he said: "the Christians."

208 – Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, informing us: Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar informed us: Shuʿbah informed us, from Simāk, who said: I heard ʿAbbād ibn Ḥubaysh narrate, from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to me: "Indeed, the astray (al-ḍāllīn) are the Christians."

209 – ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan narrated to me, saying: Muslim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Muṣʿab narrated to us, from Ḥammād ibn Salamah, from Simāk ibn Ḥarb, from Murayy ibn Qaṭarī, from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the saying of God: "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn," and he said: "The Christians are the astray."

210 – Ḥumayd ibn Masʿadah al-Sāmī narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaḍḍal narrated to us, saying: al-Jurayrī narrated to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaqīq: that a man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while he was besieging Wādī al-Qurā, and said: "I said: Who are these?" He said: "These are the astray: the Christians."

211 – Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to us, saying: Ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us, from Saʿīd al-Jurayrī, from ʿUrwah – that is, Ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qays – from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaqīq, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), with something similar.

212 – al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated to us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Budayl al-ʿUqaylī, who said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaqīq informed me, that someone who heard the Prophet (ﷺ) – while he was at Wādī al-Qurā, on his horse – informed him, and a man from the Banū al-Qayn asked him: "O Messenger of God, who are these?" – He said: "These are the astray," meaning the Christians.

213 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Khālid al-Wāsiṭī narrated to us, from Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaqīq, that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was besieging Wādī al-Qurā, while on a horse: "Who are these?" He said: "The astray," meaning the Christians.

214 – Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Mihrān narrated to us, from Sufyān, from Mujāhid: "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn," he said: the Christians.

215 – Abū Kurayb narrated to us, saying: ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd narrated to us, from Bishr ibn ʿUmārah, who said: Abū Rawq narrated to us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn," he said: "and other than the path of the Christians whom God misguided because of their fabrication against Him." He said: He says: "Inspire us with Your true religion, which is 'There is no god but God,' alone, with no partner, so that You are not angry with us as You were angry with the Jews, and do not let us go astray as You let the Christians go astray, so that You punish us with what You punish them with. He says: protect us from that by Your kindness, Your mercy and Your power."

216 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "al-ḍāllīn" are the Christians.

217 – Mūsā ibn Hārūn al-Hamdānī narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Ḥammād narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ ibn Naṣr narrated to us, from Ismāʿīl al-Suddī, in a report he mentioned from Abū Mālik, and from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās – and from Murrah al-Hamdānī, from Ibn Masʿūd – and from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn" are the Christians.

Abu Ja'far said: Every one who deviates from the direct path and travels other than the upright course is "ḍāll" (astray) in the view of the Arabs, because he has lost the way. For this reason God, mighty is His remembrance, named the Christians "ḍulāl" (the strayers), because of their error in the truth regarding the path of the right way, and their taking from the religion in a way other than the straight path.

If someone says: Is this not also a characteristic of the Jews?

It is said: Yes indeed!

If he says: Why then did He single out the Christians with this characteristic, and single out the Jews with what He described them as, that they are "those who have earned anger"?

It is said: Both groups are astray and have earned anger, except that God, His praise be exalted, marks each group with a characteristic by which His servants recognize them, when He mentions them to them or informs them about them. He did not name either group except by what is genuinely its attribute, though it has, in addition, further attributes of blame.

Some of the dull-witted of the Qadariyyah think that in God's describing the Christians as astray, with His saying "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn," and in His attributing the straying to them rather than attributing their leading astray to Himself, and in His not describing them as "those who are led astray" as He described the Jews as "those who have earned anger," there is evidence for the correctness of what their fellow ignorant Qadariyyah have said—out of ignorance of the breadth of Arabic speech and the varieties of its expressions.

Had the matter been as that dull-witted one whose situation we have described supposed, it would necessarily follow that the condition of everything described by an attribute or attributed to an act would be such that it could not have a cause for something else, and that everything in which there is something caused by something else must be attributed to its causer. Were that obligatory, it would be necessary that the saying "the tree moved" be wrong, since the winds moved it; and "the earth shook," since the earthquake moved it; and similar speech which would take too long to enumerate in this book.

And in God's saying: ﴿Until when you are in the ships and they sail with them﴾ [Surah Yūnus: 22]—by His attributing the sailing to the ships, though their sailing is by the propulsion of something else—there is evidence against the interpretation of the one whose view we have described regarding His saying "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn," and his claim that in God's attributing straying to those to whom He attributed it, the Christians, there is confirmation of what the deniers claim: that God has in the actions of His creatures a cause by which their actions come into being. Yet God, mighty is His remembrance, has made clear explicitly in many verses of His revelation that He is the One who misguides and guides. Among them is His saying: ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his desire as his god, and God has led him astray with knowledge, and has sealed his hearing and his heart, and placed over his sight a covering? Who then will guide him after God? Will you not remember?﴾ [Surah al-Jāthiyah: 23]. Thus He informed that He alone is the One who misguides and guides, and no other.

But the Qur'an was revealed in the tongue of the Arabs, as we explained at the beginning of the book, and it is a feature of the Arabs to attribute an act to the one in whom it is found, even though its real cause is other than him, and sometimes to attribute it to its real cause even though the one in whom the act is found is other than him. How much more so with an act which the servant acquires by acquisition, while God, mighty is His praise, brings its substance into existence and originates it? Rather, it is more fitting that it be attributed to the one who acquires it, as his acquisition, by the power he has over it and his choice regarding it—and to God, mighty is His praise, by bringing its essence into existence and originating it as a matter of management.

**[Question which the atheists who criticize the Qur'an ask]**

If one of them asks us and says: You have stated at the beginning of this book, in describing eloquence, that its highest degree and noblest rank is the one most effective in conveying the need of the speaker about himself, most clear about the intent of its speaker, and closest to the understanding of its hearer. You also said, with that, that the most fitting of eloquence to be like this is the speech of God, mighty is His praise, for its excellence over all other speech and the elevation of its rank above the highest degrees of eloquence [see what has passed: 9–11]. So what is the purpose—given that the matter is as you describe—of prolonging speech with something like the Mother of the Qur'an with seven verses? Two of its verses contain all its meanings, and they are His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment; You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾. For whoever knows "Master of the Day of Judgment" has known Him by His beautiful names and His exalted attributes. And whoever is obedient to God is undoubtedly following the path of those upon whom God has bestowed favour in their religion, and turning away from the path of those upon whom He has been angry and who have gone astray. So what is the wisdom in the additional five remaining verses which the two verses we mentioned did not contain?

It is said to him: God, mighty is His remembrance, gathered for our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and for his community, by what He sent down to him of His Book, meanings which He did not gather in a book He sent down to a prophet before him, or to any nation before them. That is because every book God, mighty is His remembrance, sent down to one of His prophets before him was sent down with only some of the meanings which His Book sent down to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) comprises in full. Like the Torah, which is admonition and detail; the Psalms, which is praise and glorification; and the Gospel, which is admonition and reminder—there is no miracle in any one of them that testifies to the one to whom it was sent down as being true. The Book sent down to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) comprises the meanings of all of that, and adds to it many meanings of which the other books are devoid.

We have already mentioned them earlier in this book [see what has passed: 71].

Among the most noble of those meanings by which our Book excels all books before it is its wondrous composition and its strange arrangement [in the printed edition: "and its description"; *ruṣf* means to join some of a thing to others and arrange it until it is even, firm and well-ordered], and its marvelous assembly, which orators could not match even the smallest of its sūrahs by composing, and whose description of the form of some of it eloquent people could not reach, and in whose assembly poets were bewildered, and whose understanding the intellects of the intelligent were dulled to the point of failing to produce its like, so that they found nothing but acceptance and acknowledgment that it is from the One, the Subduer. Along with that, it contains meanings which are encouragement and warning, command and prohibition, narrative, argument and parable, and similar meanings which have not been gathered in any book sent down to the earth from heaven.

Whatever length there may be in it, in the manner of the Mother of the Qur'an, is due to what I described before: that God, mighty is His remembrance, willed to gather—by its wondrous arrangement and its strange composition, which deviates from the metres of poetry, the rhymed prose of soothsayers, the sermons of orators and the letters of eloquent people, and which all of mankind is unable to arrange in a like manner, and all of the servants unable to compose its equivalent—the indication of the prophethood of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ); and, by what it contains of praise, glorification and commendation of him, to alert the servants to His greatness, sovereignty, power and the magnitude of His dominion, so that they may remember Him for His bounties and praise Him for His blessings, thereby deserving from Him more, and meriting from Him a great reward; and, by what it contains of describing the one upon whom He has bestowed the knowledge of Him and graciously granted him success in obeying Him, to inform His servants that every blessing they have in their religion and their worldly life is from Him, so that they direct their desire to Him, and seek their needs from Him alone, rather than from what is other than Him of gods and rivals; and, by what it mentions of the punishments He has brought upon those who disobeyed Him and the penalties He has sent down upon those who opposed His command—to warn His servants against committing His disobediences and exposing themselves to what they have no power to withstand of His wrath, so that He may guide them, through retribution and vengeance, along the way of those who committed such things to destruction.

This is the reason for the extended exposition in the Sūrah of the Mother of the Qur'an, and in what is similar to it among the other sūrahs of the Furqān. That is the far-reaching wisdom and the complete proof.
